questions.sub: Vision: Optics, Refraction, Accommodation, and Refractive Errors
questions.q: Which ocular structure provides approximately two-thirds (~40 to 43 diopters) of the total refractive power of the human eye (~60 diopters)?
options: Anterior surface of the cornea (air-cornea interface)
Crystalline lens
Vitreous humor
Aqueous humor
questions.explain: Because the largest jump in refractive index occurs between air (1.00) and the cornea (1.376), the cornea provides ~42 D of fixed refractive power, whereas the lens provides ~18-20 D of adjustable accommodation.

open.q: Which structure of the eye provides the greatest fixed fraction (~two-thirds) of its total refractive power?
accept: Anterior surface of the cornea
Cornea

questions.sub: Vision: Optics, Refraction, Accommodation, and Refractive Errors
questions.q: How does parasympathetic stimulation via the oculomotor nerve (CN III -> ciliary ganglion -> short ciliary nerves) produce near accommodation?
options: Ciliary muscle contracts, slackening the zonular fibers so the lens becomes more convex
Ciliary muscle contracts, tightening the zonular fibers so the lens becomes flatter
Ciliary muscle relaxes, slackening the zonular fibers so the lens becomes more convex
Radial iris muscle contracts, pulling the lens forward
questions.explain: Unlike most ligaments, zonular fibers are under resting tension when the ciliary muscle is relaxed (far vision); ciliary muscle contraction slackens the zonules, letting the elastic lens bulge to increase refractive power.

open.q: Explain the mechanical sequence by which ciliary muscle contraction increases the refractive power of the crystalline lens during near accommodation.
accept: Ciliary muscle contraction pulls the ciliary body forward/inward, slackening the zonular suspensory ligaments and allowing the elastic lens to bulge into a rounder, more convex shape
Ciliary muscle contraction relaxes zonular tension so the elastic lens thickens and becomes more convex

questions.sub: Vision: Optics, Refraction, Accommodation, and Refractive Errors
questions.q: What are the three simultaneous components of the 'near response (accommodation triad)' when shifting gaze from a distant object to a near book?
options: Lens accommodation (increased lens convexity), pupillary constriction (miosis), and medial convergence of both eyes
Lens flattening, pupillary dilation (mydriasis), and ocular divergence
Corneal flattening, ptosis, and downward gaze
Increased intraocular pressure, mydriasis, and nystagmus
questions.explain: The near triad combines lens thickening (ciliary muscle), pupillary constriction (sphincter pupillae, increasing depth of field), and ocular convergence (bilateral medial recti).

open.q: Name the three physiological responses that constitute the visual 'near triad' when focusing on a close object.
accept: Lens accommodation (thickening), pupillary constriction (miosis), and ocular convergence
Accommodation, miosis, and convergence

questions.sub: Vision: Optics, Refraction, Accommodation, and Refractive Errors
questions.q: Contrast the optical focal point and corrective lens type for 'myopia (nearsightedness)' versus 'hyperopia (farsightedness)':
options: Myopia focuses images in front of the retina and is corrected with a diverging lens; hyperopia focuses images behind it and is corrected with a converging lens
Myopia focuses images behind the retina and needs a converging lens; hyperopia focuses images in front and needs a diverging lens
Both conditions focus images on the retina but require cylindrical lenses
Myopia and hyperopia both result from unequal corneal curvature and require cylindrical lenses
questions.explain: A diverging biconcave (-) lens spreads incoming rays slightly so a myopic eye focuses them back onto the retina; a converging biconvex (+) lens adds focusing power to bring hyperopic rays forward onto the retina.

open.q: State where parallel light rays focus relative to the retina and which corrective lens shape is used in myopia versus hyperopia.
accept: Myopia: focuses in front of the retina, corrected with a biconcave (diverging) lens; Hyperopia: focuses behind the retina, corrected with a biconvex (converging) lens
Myopia: in front of retina, concave lens; Hyperopia: behind retina, convex lens

questions.sub: Vision: Optics, Refraction, Accommodation, and Refractive Errors
questions.q: What causes 'presbyopia' in adults over age 45, and what causes 'astigmatism'?
options: Presbyopia: stiffened lens; astigmatism: unequal corneal/lenticular meridians (cylindrical correction)
Presbyopia is caused by elongation of the optic nerve; Astigmatism is caused by vitamin A deficiency
Presbyopia is corrected with cylindrical lenses; Astigmatism is corrected with prism lenses
Both are caused by detachment of the macula lutea
questions.explain: Even though ciliary muscle contraction persists in presbyopia, the hardened lens nucleus can no longer round up; astigmatism requires cylindrical lenses oriented along the defective meridian. Key detail: Presbyopia: progressive age-related loss of crystalline lens elasticity reducing accommodation amplitude for near reading; Astigmatism: asymmetric/toric curvature of the cornea or lens causing different meridians to focus at different planes, corrected with a CYLINDRICAL lens.

open.q: Distinguish the anatomical cause of presbyopia from that of astigmatism, and state the corrective lens used for astigmatism.
accept: Presbyopia: age-related stiffening/loss of elasticity of the crystalline lens; Astigmatism: unequal curvature of the cornea or lens across different meridians, corrected with a cylindrical lens
Presbyopia: loss of lens elasticity; Astigmatism: asymmetric corneal/lens curvature corrected by cylindrical lenses

questions.sub: Vision: Aqueous Humor, Intraocular Pressure, and Glaucoma
questions.q: Trace the normal production and drainage pathway of 'aqueous humor' that maintains intraocular pressure (normal 10-21 mmHg):
options: Ciliary processes → posterior chamber → pupil → anterior chamber → trabecular meshwork → canal of Schlemm → episcleral veins
Lacrimal gland → conjunctival sac → nasolacrimal duct → inferior meatus → nasal cavity
Ciliary processes → anterior chamber → vitreous body → central retinal vein
Choroid → posterior chamber → optic canal → cavernous sinus
questions.explain: Aqueous humor nourishes the avascular lens and cornea; obstruction at the pupil or trabecular meshwork elevates intraocular pressure (glaucoma) and compresses optic nerve head axons.

open.q: Trace the anatomical pathway of aqueous humor from its site of secretion to its primary venous drainage.
accept: Ciliary processes (posterior chamber) -> through pupil into anterior chamber -> trabecular meshwork at iridocorneal angle -> canal of Schlemm -> episcleral veins
Ciliary body -> posterior chamber -> pupil -> anterior chamber -> trabecular meshwork -> canal of Schlemm -> episcleral veins

questions.sub: Vision: Retinal Layers, Rods vs Cones, and Phototransduction
questions.q: Why must light pass through the inner retinal neural layers before reaching the photoreceptor outer segments, and how is this anatomical arrangement modified at the 'fovea centralis'?
options: Photoreceptors face the retinal pigment epithelium; at the fovea, inner retinal layers are displaced to reduce light scattering
Photoreceptors face the vitreous; at the fovea, ganglion cells form an extra layer over the cones
The retinal pigment epithelium lies anterior to the neural retina and is absent at the fovea
Foveal cones are covered by dense retinal capillaries that focus incoming light
questions.explain: At the fovea centralis, lateral displacement of ganglion/bipolar layers, absence of overlying blood vessels, and 1:1 cone-to-ganglion cell wiring yield maximal spatial resolution.

open.q: Explain two anatomical specializations of the fovea centralis that give it the highest visual acuity in the human retina.
accept: Lateral displacement of inner retinal layers and overlying blood vessels so light strikes densely packed cones directly, plus 1:1 private-line convergence from cones to bipolar and ganglion cells
Absence of overlying inner retinal layers/blood vessels and high density of cones with 1:1 ganglion cell wiring

questions.sub: Vision: Retinal Layers, Rods vs Cones, and Phototransduction
questions.q: Compare the functional properties of retinal 'rods' versus 'cones':
options: Rods provide sensitive, low-acuity scotopic vision mainly peripherally; cones provide high-acuity, color photopic vision, concentrated centrally
Rods provide high-acuity color vision centrally; cones provide sensitive monochromatic vision mainly peripherally
Rods and cones are equally concentrated at the fovea and have similar light sensitivity
Rods mediate daylight color vision; cones mediate dim-light peripheral vision
questions.explain: High convergence onto bipolar cells amplifies faint photon signals in rods (high sensitivity, low spatial resolution), whereas 1:1 wiring in foveal cones sacrifices sensitivity for crisp detail and color.

open.q: Contrast rods and cones in terms of light sensitivity, spatial acuity, retinal distribution, and neural convergence.
accept: Rods: high sensitivity for dim/scotopic vision, low acuity due to high neural convergence, concentrated in peripheral retina; Cones: lower sensitivity for bright/photopic and color vision, high acuity due to low (1:1) convergence, concentrated in the fovea
Rods: dim-light, high convergence, peripheral, low acuity; Cones: bright-light/color, low convergence, foveal, high acuity

questions.sub: Vision: Retinal Layers, Rods vs Cones, and Phototransduction
questions.q: What is the unique electrophysiological response of vertebrate rod and cone photoreceptors when struck by light ('phototransduction cascade')?
options: Light activates transducin and phosphodiesterase, lowers cGMP, closes cation channels, and hyperpolarizes the photoreceptor
Light inhibits transducin, raises cGMP, opens cation channels, and depolarizes the photoreceptor
Light activates adenylyl cyclase, raises cAMP, opens sodium channels, and triggers action potentials
Light opens voltage-gated sodium channels directly, causing photoreceptors to fire action potentials
questions.explain: Unlike almost all other sensory receptors, photoreceptors are depolarized in the DARK (via continuous cGMP-gated Na+/Ca2+ 'dark current') and HYPERPOLARIZE in the LIGHT, reducing glutamate release onto bipolar cells.

open.q: Trace the intracellular signaling steps from photon absorption by rhodopsin to hyperpolarization of a rod photoreceptor.
accept: 11-cis-retinal isomerizes to all-trans-retinal -> activates transducin (Gt) -> activates cGMP phosphodiesterase (PDE) -> hydrolyzes cGMP -> closes cGMP-gated Na+/Ca2+ channels -> membrane hyperpolarization and decreased glutamate release
Isomerization of 11-cis-retinal activates transducin and PDE, lowering cGMP to close Na+/Ca2+ channels and hyperpolarize the cell

questions.sub: Vision: Retinal Layers, Rods vs Cones, and Phototransduction
questions.q: How does light-induced hyperpolarization of a photoreceptor excite an 'ON-center bipolar cell' while inhibiting an 'OFF-center bipolar cell'?
options: Reduced glutamate removes mGluR6-mediated inhibition from ON cells but reduces AMPA/kainate excitation of OFF cells
Reduced glutamate activates mGluR6 on ON cells but removes inhibition from AMPA receptors on OFF cells
Increased glutamate excites ON cells through AMPA receptors and inhibits OFF cells through mGluR6
Both ON and OFF bipolar cells depolarize because they express the same glutamate receptors
questions.explain: Receptor sign-inversion via mGluR6 on ON-bipolar cells splits every retinal point into parallel ON and OFF contrast channels before signals even reach retinal ganglion cells.

open.q: Explain why a decrease in photoreceptor glutamate release depolarizes ON-center bipolar cells but hyperpolarizes OFF-center bipolar cells.
accept: ON-center bipolar cells use inhibitory metabotropic mGluR6 receptors (so less glutamate relieves inhibition and depolarizes them), whereas OFF-center bipolar cells use excitatory ionotropic AMPA/kainate receptors (so less glutamate hyperpolarizes them)
Inhibitory mGluR6 receptors on ON-bipolar cells vs excitatory ionotropic AMPA/kainate receptors on OFF-bipolar cells

questions.sub: Vision: Retinal Layers, Rods vs Cones, and Phototransduction
questions.q: Which retinal neurons are the ONLY cells in the retina that normally generate all-or-none propagated action potentials, and whose axons form the optic nerve (CN II)?
options: Retinal ganglion cells
Rod and cone photoreceptors
Horizontal cells
Bipolar cells
questions.explain: Photoreceptors, horizontal cells, and bipolar cells communicate via graded electrotonic potentials; retinal ganglion cells (plus some amacrine cells) generate true Na+ action potentials transmitted along the optic nerve.

open.q: Which retinal cell type generates propagated action potentials and sends its axons out of the eye to form the optic nerve?
accept: Retinal ganglion cells
Ganglion cells

questions.sub: Vision: Retinal Layers, Rods vs Cones, and Phototransduction
questions.q: What explains the biphasic 'dark adaptation curve' (initial rapid drop in visual threshold over 5-10 minutes followed by a slower, deeper drop over 20-30 minutes) when entering a dark room?
options: Cones regenerate quickly (first phase); rods regenerate rhodopsin slowly to maximal dark sensitivity
The first phase is pupillary dilation and the second phase is lens thickening
Rods regenerate within 30 seconds while cones require 45 minutes
The biphasic curve is caused by blinking every 10 minutes
questions.explain: Cones regenerate photopsin quickly but plateau at a higher light threshold; rods regenerate rhodopsin slowly over 20-30 minutes to reach maximum scotopic sensitivity. Key detail: The initial rapid phase reflects fast regeneration of CONE photopigments (reaching cone threshold at ~7-10 min), whereas the second slower phase reflects gradual regeneration of ROD rhodopsin (rod-cone break), which achieves ~10,000-fold greater dark sensitivity after ~30 minutes.

open.q: Explain the physiological basis of the two phases of the human dark adaptation curve separated by the rod-cone break.
accept: The early rapid phase reflects faster regeneration of cone photopigments (reaching cone sensitivity limit in ~5-10 min), while the slower second phase reflects gradual regeneration of rod rhodopsin to achieve maximum scotopic sensitivity (~20-30 min)
Fast cone photopigment regeneration (first phase) followed by slower rod rhodopsin regeneration (second phase)

questions.sub: Vision: Visual Pathways, Field Defects, and Pupillary Light Reflex
questions.q: Which retinal ganglion cell axons decussate (cross to the contralateral side) at the 'optic chiasm'?
options: Axons from the NASAL hemiretinas of both eyes (which view the TEMPORAL visual fields), while temporal hemiretinal fibers remain ipsilateral
Axons from the temporal hemiretinas of both eyes
All axons from the left eye cross while all axons from the right eye stay ipsilateral
Only axons from the superior half of each retina
questions.explain: Because nasal hemiretina fibers cross at the optic chiasm while temporal hemiretina fibers stay uncrossed, the right optic tract carries the entire LEFT visual field from both eyes.

open.q: Which retinal fibers cross at the optic chiasm and which visual fields do they represent?
accept: Nasal hemiretinal fibers from both eyes cross at the optic chiasm; they carry information from the bilateral temporal visual fields
Nasal retinal fibers (representing the temporal visual fields)

questions.sub: Vision: Visual Pathways, Field Defects, and Pupillary Light Reflex
questions.q: Match the visual pathway lesion site with its characteristic visual field defect: (1) Right optic nerve, (2) Optic chiasm, (3) Right optic tract, (4) Right temporal Meyer's loop:
options: (1) Right monocular blindness; (2) Bitemporal hemianopsia; (3) Left homonymous hemianopsia; (4) Left superior homonymous quadrantanopia ('pie in the sky')
(1) Bitemporal hemianopsia; (2) Right monocular blindness; (3) Right homonymous hemianopsia; (4) Left inferior quadrantanopia
(1) Left homonymous hemianopsia; (2) Binasal hemianopsia; (3) Central scotoma; (4) Total blindness
(1) Right superior quadrantanopia; (2) Left monocular blindness; (3) Bitemporal hemianopsia; (4) Macular sparing
questions.explain: Pre-chiasmal = monocular loss; chiasmal = bitemporal hemianopsia; retro-chiasmal right side = contralateral (left) homonymous deficit; temporal Meyer's loop carries inferior retinal fibers (= superior visual field).

open.q: State the visual field defects caused by lesions of: (a) the optic chiasm, (b) the right optic tract, and (c) the right temporal Meyer's loop.
accept: (a) Bitemporal hemianopsia; (b) Left homonymous hemianopsia; (c) Left superior homonymous quadrantanopia ('pie in the sky')
Bitemporal hemianopsia, left homonymous hemianopsia, and left superior quadrantanopia

questions.sub: Vision: Visual Pathways, Field Defects, and Pupillary Light Reflex
questions.q: Trace the neural pathway of the 'pupillary light reflex' (direct and consensual constriction) when light is shone into the right eye:
options: Retina → optic nerve/chiasm/tract → pretectal nuclei → bilateral Edinger–Westphal nuclei → CN III → ciliary ganglia → sphincter pupillae
Retina → optic tract → lateral geniculate nucleus → visual cortex → unilateral Edinger–Westphal nucleus → CN III
Retina → superior colliculus → facial nucleus → CN VII → ciliary ganglion → dilator pupillae
Retina → optic nerve → medial geniculate nucleus → bilateral vestibular nuclei → CN VI → sphincter pupillae
questions.explain: Bilateral projections from each pretectal nucleus to BOTH Edinger-Westphal nuclei explain why shining light into one eye constricts both the stimulated eye (direct reflex) and the unstimulated eye (consensual reflex).

open.q: Trace the afferent and efferent neural pathway of the pupillary light reflex and explain why shining light into one eye causes consensual constriction of the opposite pupil.
accept: Retina -> optic nerve (CN II) -> optic tract -> pretectal nucleus -> bilateral Edinger-Westphal nuclei -> bilateral CN III -> ciliary ganglion -> short ciliary nerves -> iris sphincter pupillae; bilateral innervation of both Edinger-Westphal nuclei produces consensual constriction
CN II -> pretectal nucleus -> bilateral Edinger-Westphal nuclei -> bilateral CN III -> ciliary ganglion -> sphincter pupillae

questions.sub: Vision: Visual Pathways, Field Defects, and Pupillary Light Reflex
questions.q: What is a 'Relative Afferent Pupillary Defect (RAPD / Marcus Gunn pupil)' on the swinging flashlight test, and what does it localize to?
options: RAPD: both pupils relatively dilate when light swings to the affected eye, indicating optic nerve/retinal afferent loss
Paralysis of the iris sphincter due to oculomotor nerve (CN III) compression
Failure of pupillary constriction to light with preserved constriction to near vision (neurosyphilis)
Ipsilateral ptosis, miosis, and anhidrosis from sympathetic lesion
questions.explain: Because an RAPD is an AFFERENT defect, both pupils respond identically during the test: strong bilateral constriction when light hits the intact eye, followed by bilateral relative dilation when light swings to the damaged optic nerve. Key detail: When swinging a bright light from the healthy eye to the affected eye, BOTH pupils paradoxically dilate instead of staying constricted—indicating asymmetric afferent damage in the ipsilateral optic nerve (CN II) or severe retinal disease.

open.q: Describe the pupillary response during a positive swinging flashlight test (Marcus Gunn pupil) and identify the anatomical site of the lesion.
accept: Both pupils constrict briskly when light is shone into the normal eye, but both paradoxically dilate when light swings onto the affected eye; localizes to an asymmetric afferent lesion of the ipsilateral optic nerve (CN II) or severe retinal disease
Paradoxical bilateral pupillary dilation when swinging light from the healthy eye to the affected eye; ipsilateral optic nerve (CN II) or severe retinal lesion

questions.sub: Vision: Visual Pathways, Field Defects, and Pupillary Light Reflex
questions.q: Compare 'Argyll Robertson pupil' with 'oculomotor nerve (CN III) palsy' regarding pupillary light and near accommodation responses:
options: Argyll Robertson pupils fail to react to light but constrict for near vision; a compressive CN III palsy typically causes a dilated, poorly reactive pupil with ptosis and a down-and-out eye
Argyll Robertson pupils are dilated and fail to accommodate; CN III palsy causes pinpoint pupils with preserved eye movement
Both conditions cause small pupils with absent near responses and normal extraocular movement
Argyll Robertson pupils are caused by optic nerve damage; CN III palsy causes bitemporal hemianopia
questions.explain: In Argyll Robertson pupil ('prostitute's pupil': accommodates but does not react), dorsal midbrain pretectal light-reflex fibers are damaged while more ventral cortical near-accommodation fibers to Edinger-Westphal are spared.

open.q: Define 'light-near dissociation' in an Argyll Robertson pupil and state its classic underlying etiology and lesion site.
accept: Pupils fail to constrict to direct light but constrict normally during near accommodation; classically caused by tertiary neurosyphilis damaging the dorsal midbrain pretectal region while sparing ventral near-accommodation pathways
Absent pupillary light reflex with preserved near accommodation reflex; dorsal midbrain pretectal lesion in neurosyphilis

questions.sub: Vision: Retinal Layers, Rods vs Cones, and Phototransduction
questions.q: How does 'lateral inhibition' mediated by retinal 'horizontal cells' sharpen visual edges and enhance contrast (Mach bands)?
options: Illumination reduces photoreceptor glutamate release, hyperpolarizing horizontal cells and weakening lateral inhibition around the stimulated area
Illumination increases photoreceptor glutamate release, depolarizing horizontal cells and strengthening inhibition at the stimulated center
Horizontal cells sharpen edges by directly exciting all neighboring ganglion cells with acetylcholine
Horizontal cells suppress contrast by preventing photoreceptors from releasing glutamate in darkness
questions.explain: Center-surround antagonism created by horizontal cell lateral inhibition makes retinal ganglion cells respond vigorously to edges and luminance contrasts rather than uniform illumination.

open.q: Which retinal interneurons mediate lateral inhibition between adjacent photoreceptors to create center-surround receptive fields and sharpen visual edges?
accept: Horizontal cells
Retinal horizontal cells

questions.sub: Vision: Visual Pathways, Field Defects, and Pupillary Light Reflex
questions.q: Contrast the 'magnocellular (M-pathway)' and 'parvocellular (P-pathway)' streams from the retina through the lateral geniculate nucleus (LGN) to the visual cortex:
options: M: motion/depth, LGN layers 1–2 → dorsal stream; P: fine form/colour, layers 3–6 → ventral stream
Magnocellular pathways process red-green color while parvocellular pathways detect rapid motion
Both M and P pathways bypass the LGN and terminate in the cochlea
Parvocellular layers are layers 1 and 2 of the LGN
questions.explain: Remember: M = Motion / Magnocellular / LGN layers 1-2 -> Dorsal ('where'); P = Parvocellular / LGN layers 3-6 -> Ventral ('what': pattern, form, color). Key detail: Magnocellular (LGN layers 1-2 -> dorsal 'where/how' parietal stream): large receptive fields, fast conduction, high contrast sensitivity, specialized for MOTION and depth detection; Parvocellular (LGN layers 3-6 -> ventral 'what' temporal stream): small receptive fields, slow conduction, specialized for fine spatial FORM and red-green COLOR vision.

open.q: Distinguish the functional specializations and cortical destinations (dorsal vs ventral streams) of the magnocellular and parvocellular visual pathways.
accept: Magnocellular pathway (LGN layers 1-2 -> dorsal parietal 'where/how' stream): detects motion, depth, and low-contrast luminance; Parvocellular pathway (LGN layers 3-6 -> ventral temporal 'what' stream): processes fine spatial form, pattern, and red-green color
Magnocellular: motion/depth via dorsal stream; Parvocellular: fine form/color via ventral stream

questions.sub: Vision: Visual Pathways, Field Defects, and Pupillary Light Reflex
questions.q: Which non-visual retinal photoreceptors project via the 'retinohypothalamic tract' to the 'suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN)' of the hypothalamus to entrain circadian rhythms and suppress pineal melatonin secretion?
options: Intrinsically photosensitive retinal ganglion cells (ipRGCs) containing the blue-light-sensitive photopigment melanopsin
Peripheral rod photoreceptors containing rhodopsin
L-cones containing erythrolabe
Amacrine cells containing dopamine
questions.explain: Melanopsin-expressing ipRGCs (~480 nm blue light sensitivity) project directly to the SCN (master circadian clock) and pretectal nuclei, explaining why blind individuals lacking rods/cones can still maintain circadian entrainment.

open.q: Name the retinal cells, photopigment, and hypothalamic target nucleus responsible for light-induced entrainment of circadian rhythms.
accept: Intrinsically photosensitive retinal ganglion cells (ipRGCs) expressing melanopsin projecting via the retinohypothalamic tract to the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN)
Melanopsin-containing retinal ganglion cells (ipRGCs) -> suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN)

questions.sub: Audition: Tympanic Membrane, Ossicles, and Impedance Matching
questions.q: How does the middle ear (tympanic membrane + malleus, incus, stapes) solve the 'acoustic impedance mismatch' between low-impedance air and high-impedance cochlear perilymph?
options: The larger tympanic membrane area and ossicular lever concentrate force onto the smaller stapes footplate, increasing pressure at the oval window
The smaller tympanic membrane and larger stapes footplate increase sound pressure by spreading force across a wider area
The ossicles amplify sound by generating action potentials in the malleus before vibrations reach the cochlea
The Eustachian tube increases cochlear pressure by pumping air directly into the scala vestibuli
questions.explain: Without middle ear impedance matching, 99.9% (~30 dB) of airborne sound energy would bounce off the dense cochlear fluid interface; area concentration (~17x) times lever ratio (~1.3x) yields ~22x pressure amplification.

open.q: Explain the two mechanical mechanisms by which the middle ear achieves impedance matching and state the resulting pressure amplification factor at the oval window.
accept: 1) Hydraulic area ratio (~17:1) between the large tympanic membrane and small stapes footplate, and 2) ossicular lever ratio (~1.3:1) between malleus and incus, yielding ~22-fold (~27 dB) pressure amplification
Area ratio (~17:1) and ossicular lever ratio (~1.3:1), amplifying pressure ~22-fold

questions.sub: Audition: Tympanic Membrane, Ossicles, and Impedance Matching
questions.q: What is the 'tympanic (acoustic/attenuation) reflex', which muscles and cranial nerves mediate it, and what is its physiological function?
options: Loud sound contracts tensor tympani (CN V3) and stapedius (CN VII), stiffening the ossicles and reducing mainly low-frequency transmission
Loud sound contracts tensor tympani (CN VII) and stapedius (CN V3), loosening the ossicles and amplifying low-frequency transmission
Quiet sound contracts stapedius (CN IX) and tensor tympani (CN X), opening the oval window
Loud sound relaxes both middle-ear muscles, increasing stapes movement to protect cochlear hair cells
questions.explain: Because the acoustic reflex has a ~40-80 ms synaptic latency, it protects against sustained loud noise and chewing/speaking sounds, though it cannot protect against sudden impulsive gunshots; CN VII palsy paralyzes the stapedius, causing painful 'hyperacusis'.

open.q: Name the two middle ear muscles of the acoustic attenuation reflex, their respective cranial nerve innervations, and the clinical symptom when the stapedius is paralyzed.
accept: Tensor tympani (mandibular trigeminal nerve, CN V3) and stapedius (facial nerve, CN VII); stapedius paralysis causes hyperacusis (painful sensitivity to everyday sounds)
Tensor tympani (CN V3) and stapedius (CN VII); hyperacusis

questions.sub: Audition: Tympanic Membrane, Ossicles, and Impedance Matching
questions.q: What is the primary physiological function of the 'Eustachian (pharyngotympanic) tube'?
options: Equalises middle-ear and nasopharyngeal pressure during swallowing or yawning
Conducts endolymph from the cochlea to the oral cavity
Transmits sound vibrations directly from the pharynx to the auditory cortex
Secretes cerumen into the external auditory canal
questions.explain: If the Eustachian tube is blocked (e.g., upper respiratory infection or rapid airplane descent), trapped middle ear air is absorbed, creating negative pressure that retracts the tympanic membrane and causes conductive hearing loss. Key detail: Periodically opens during swallowing or yawning (via tensor veli palatini) to equalize air pressure between the middle ear cavity and nasopharynx so the tympanic membrane remains free to vibrate symmetrically.

open.q: State the physiological role of the Eustachian tube in middle ear mechanics.
accept: Equalizes air pressure across the tympanic membrane between the middle ear cavity and the nasopharynx so the eardrum can vibrate optimally
Equalizes middle ear pressure with atmospheric nasopharyngeal pressure

questions.sub: Audition: Cochlear Mechanics, Organ of Corti, and Hair Cell Transduction
questions.q: Compare the fluid compartments, ionic composition, and electrical potential of cochlear 'perilymph' versus 'endolymph':
options: Perilymph: high Na+, low K+, ~0 mV; endolymph: high K+, low Na+, +80 mV
Endolymph has high Na+ and -90 mV potential while perilymph has high K+
Both scala vestibuli and scala media contain blood plasma
Endolymph is secreted by the tympanic membrane
questions.explain: Because endolymph has +80 mV potential and hair cell cytoplasm is ~-60 to -70 mV, there is a massive ~140-150 mV electrical driving force pushing K+ INTO hair cells when apical transduction channels open! Key detail: Perilymph (fills scala vestibuli and scala tympani; continuous with CSF): high Na+ (~140 mM), low K+ (~4-5 mM), 0 mV; Endolymph (fills scala media / cochlear duct; secreted by stria vascularis): uniquely high K+ (~150 mM), low Na+ (~1 mM), and a +80 mV endocochlear potential.

open.q: Contrast cochlear endolymph and perilymph in terms of their locations, dominant cation (Na+ vs K+), and electrical potential.
accept: Endolymph: inside scala media, high K+ (~150 mM) and low Na+, +80 mV endocochlear potential (secreted by stria vascularis); Perilymph: inside scala vestibuli and scala tympani, high Na+ and low K+ (like CSF/ECF), 0 mV
Endolymph (scala media, high K+, +80 mV) vs Perilymph (scala vestibuli/tympani, high Na+, 0 mV)

questions.sub: Audition: Cochlear Mechanics, Organ of Corti, and Hair Cell Transduction
questions.q: Why does bending cochlear hair cell stereocilia toward the tallest stereocilium (kinocilium direction) DEPOLARIZE the hair cell using K+ influx rather than Na+ influx?
options: Deflection toward the tallest stereocilia opens tip-link channels; K⁺ enters from endolymph, depolarizing the hair cell and promoting Ca²⁺-dependent glutamate release
Deflection toward the tallest stereocilia closes tip-link channels; K⁺ leaves the hair cell and reduces glutamate release
Deflection away from the tallest stereocilia opens Na⁺ channels because endolymph is sodium-rich
Stereociliary deflection opens basolateral Ca²⁺ channels first, causing K⁺ to leave through the apical surface
questions.explain: Because apical stereocilia sit in high-K+ endolymph (+80 mV) while the basolateral soma sits in low-K+ perilymph (0 mV), K+ enters apically to depolarize the cell and exits basolaterally into perilymph without requiring local apical Na+/K+-ATPase pumping.

open.q: Explain the ionic mechanism by which deflection of cochlear hair cell stereocilia toward the tallest stereocilium depolarizes the hair cell and triggers neurotransmitter release.
accept: Tip links pull open apical mechanotransduction channels, allowing K+ from K+-rich (+80 mV) endolymph to flow into the cell down its electrochemical gradient, depolarizing the membrane, opening basolateral voltage-gated Ca2+ channels, and triggering glutamate release
Tip-link opening of apical MET channels causes inward K+ influx from endolymph -> depolarization -> voltage-gated Ca2+ entry -> glutamate release

questions.sub: Audition: Cochlear Mechanics, Organ of Corti, and Hair Cell Transduction
questions.q: Contrast the functional roles of 'inner hair cells (IHCs)' versus 'outer hair cells (OHCs)' in the Organ of Corti:
options: Inner hair cells provide most auditory afferent input; outer hair cells amplify cochlear vibrations through prestin-mediated motility
Outer hair cells provide most auditory afferent input; inner hair cells amplify vibrations through prestin
Both cell types are purely sensory and receive no efferent innervation
Inner and outer hair cells have identical numbers, roles and neural connections
questions.explain: Inner hair cells are the true microphones (~95% of CN VIII afferent input), while prestin-powered electromotility of outer hair cells amplifies weak basilar membrane vibrations (and generates otoacoustic emissions!).

open.q: Distinguish the primary roles of cochlear inner hair cells and outer hair cells, naming the motor protein responsible for outer hair cell electromotility.
accept: Inner hair cells are the primary afferent auditory receptors (~95% of CN VIII afferent synapses); outer hair cells act as a mechanical 'cochlear amplifier' that sharpens frequency tuning and amplifies soft sounds via prestin-mediated electromotility
Inner hair cells: primary sensory transduction (~95% afferent); Outer hair cells: cochlear amplification/tuning via prestin

questions.sub: Audition: Tonotopic Organization, Auditory Pathway, and Hearing Loss Tests
questions.q: How does the 'basilar membrane' encode sound frequency spatially ('tonotopic place coding' / von Bekesy traveling wave)?
options: Basilar membrane base: narrow/stiff/high pitch; apex: wide/compliant/low pitch
The base is wide and floppy for low frequencies while the apex is narrow and stiff for high frequencies
All sound frequencies vibrate the entire basilar membrane with identical amplitude
High frequencies are detected in the semicircular canals while low frequencies are detected in the utricle
questions.explain: Mnemonic: 'Base = High pitch (stiff/narrow, like short tight guitar strings); Apex = Low pitch (wide/floppy, like long loose bass strings).' Note that the cochlea itself is wider at its bony base, while the basilar membrane inside is narrower at the base! Key detail: The BASE of the basilar membrane (near the oval window) is NARROW and STIFF, resonating maximally to HIGH-frequency sounds (~20,000 Hz), whereas the APEX (near the helicotrema) is WIDE and FLOPPY/COMPLIANT, resonating maximally to LOW-frequency sounds (~20 Hz).

open.q: Compare the physical dimensions, stiffness, and resonant sound frequencies of the base versus the apex of the cochlear basilar membrane.
accept: Base (near oval window): narrow and stiff, maximally vibrated by high-frequency sounds (~20 kHz); Apex (near helicotrema): wide and compliant/floppy, maximally vibrated by low-frequency sounds (~20 Hz)
Base: narrow, stiff, high frequencies; Apex: wide, floppy, low frequencies

questions.sub: Audition: Tonotopic Organization, Auditory Pathway, and Hearing Loss Tests
questions.q: Trace the central ascending auditory pathway from the spiral ganglion to the primary auditory cortex ('E-COLI' mnemonic):
options: Cochlear nuclei → superior olive → lateral lemniscus → inferior colliculus → MGN → auditory cortex
Spiral ganglion -> lateral geniculate nucleus -> calcarine sulcus of occipital lobe
Spiral ganglion -> ventral posterolateral (VPL) nucleus -> postcentral gyrus
Spiral ganglion -> olfactory bulb -> piriform cortex
questions.explain: Because auditory projections cross bilaterally starting at the cochlear nuclei/superior olive, a unilateral cortical stroke in Heschl's gyrus causes bilateral difficulty localizing sounds rather than complete unilateral deafness! Key detail: Spiral ganglion (CN VIII) -> dorsal & ventral cochlear nuclei (pontomedullary junction) -> bilateral superior olivary complexes (sound localization) -> lateral lemniscus -> inferior colliculus (midbrain) -> medial geniculate nucleus (MGN) of thalamus -> primary auditory cortex (Heschl's transverse temporal gyrus, Brodmann areas 41/42).

open.q: List the sequential central relay nuclei of the ascending auditory pathway from the cochlear nuclei to the primary auditory cortex.
accept: Cochlear nuclei -> superior olivary complex -> lateral lemniscus -> inferior colliculus -> medial geniculate nucleus (MGN) of thalamus -> primary auditory cortex (Heschl's gyrus, areas 41/42)
Cochlear nuclei -> superior olive -> lateral lemniscus -> inferior colliculus -> medial geniculate body -> primary auditory cortex

questions.sub: Audition: Tonotopic Organization, Auditory Pathway, and Hearing Loss Tests
questions.q: Which brainstem auditory structure is the FIRST site to receive binaural input from both ears and compute horizontal sound localization using interaural time differences (low frequencies) and interaural intensity differences (high frequencies)?
options: Superior olivary complex (medial superior olive for interaural time delay; lateral superior olive for interaural level/intensity difference)
Lateral geniculate nucleus
Ciliary ganglion
Subthalamic nucleus
questions.explain: The medial superior olive acts as a coincidence detector for microsecond interaural arrival-time differences, whereas the lateral superior olive compares head-shadow intensity differences between the two ears.

open.q: Name the first brainstem auditory nucleus to integrate binaural inputs for sound localization and state the two binaural cues it compares.
accept: Superior olivary complex; compares interaural time differences (medial superior olive) and interaural intensity/level differences (lateral superior olive)
Superior olivary complex; interaural time difference and interaural intensity difference

questions.sub: Audition: Tonotopic Organization, Auditory Pathway, and Hearing Loss Tests
questions.q: Interpret a tuning-fork examination showing: Weber test lateralizes to the LEFT ear, and Rinne test on the LEFT ear shows Bone Conduction > Air Conduction (negative Rinne), while the RIGHT ear shows Air Conduction > Bone Conduction (positive Rinne):
options: Left-sided CONDUCTIVE hearing loss (e.g., cerumen impaction, otitis media with effusion, or otosclerosis)
Left-sided sensorineural hearing loss
Right-sided conductive hearing loss
Normal bilateral hearing
questions.explain: In conductive hearing loss, bone conduction bypasses the blocked middle/external ear and environmental room noise is masked on the affected side, making the Weber tuning fork sound LOUDER in the conductive-loss ear while Rinne shows BC > AC.

open.q: What type and side of hearing loss is diagnosed when Weber lateralizes to the left ear and Rinne on the left ear shows bone conduction greater than air conduction?
accept: Left-sided conductive hearing loss
Left conductive hearing loss

questions.sub: Audition: Tonotopic Organization, Auditory Pathway, and Hearing Loss Tests
questions.q: Interpret a tuning-fork examination showing: Weber test lateralizes to the RIGHT ear, and Rinne test shows Air Conduction > Bone Conduction (positive Rinne) in BOTH ears, though much shorter/diminished on the left:
options: Left-sided SENSORINEURAL hearing loss (cochlear or CN VIII damage)
Left-sided conductive hearing loss
Right-sided conductive hearing loss
Bilateral tympanic membrane perforation
questions.explain: In unilateral sensorineural hearing loss, the Weber fork is heard louder in the healthy ear (away from the lesion), while the affected ear retains normal AC > BC ratio (both air and bone conduction are reduced equally).

open.q: State the expected Weber and Rinne tuning-fork test findings in a patient with unilateral left-sided sensorineural hearing loss.
accept: Weber lateralizes to the right (healthy) ear; Rinne is positive (air conduction > bone conduction) bilaterally, with reduced duration on the left
Weber lateralizes to right ear; Rinne AC > BC in both ears

questions.sub: Vestibular System: Semicircular Canals, Otolith Organs, and Nystagmus
questions.q: Contrast the adequate physiological stimuli detected by the 'semicircular canals' versus the 'otolith organs (utricle and saccule)':
options: Semicircular canals: angular acceleration; utricle/saccule: linear acceleration and tilt (horizontal/vertical)
Semicircular canals detect static gravity while otolith organs detect rotational acceleration
Utricle detects sound waves at 10 kHz while saccule detects sweet taste
Both semicircular canals and otolith organs detect only constant-velocity linear motion
questions.explain: Because endolymph catches up to the canal walls during constant-velocity spinning, semicircular canals respond strictly to angular ACCELERATION/DECELERATION, whereas weighted otoconia let the utricle and saccule sense static head tilt and linear acceleration. Key detail: Semicircular canals (anterior, posterior, horizontal): detect ANGULAR (rotational) head acceleration via endolymph inertial deflection of the cupula in the crista ampullaris; Otolith organs: detect LINEAR acceleration and static head tilt relative to gravity via CaCO3 otoconia shifting the otolithic membrane over the macula (utricle = horizontal plane; saccule = vertical plane).

open.q: Contrast the stimuli detected by the semicircular canals versus the utricle and saccule, specifying the plane of orientation of each otolith organ.
accept: Semicircular canals detect angular/rotational head acceleration; Otolith organs detect linear acceleration and static head tilt relative to gravity, with the utricle oriented horizontally and the saccule oriented vertically
Semicircular canals: angular acceleration; Otolith organs: linear acceleration/gravity (utricle horizontal, saccule vertical)

questions.sub: Vestibular System: Semicircular Canals, Otolith Organs, and Nystagmus
questions.q: How does turning the head horizontally to the LEFT affect hair cell firing in the left versus right horizontal semicircular canals, and how does the 'vestibulo-ocular reflex (VOR)' keep your gaze fixed on a target?
options: Left head turn excites the left horizontal canal, inhibits the right; the VOR drives the eyes right
Turning the head left inhibits both horizontal semicircular canals equally
The VOR rotates the eyes in the exact same direction (left) as the head turn
In the horizontal semicircular canal, stereocilia bend away from the kinocilium to cause depolarization
questions.explain: In the horizontal semicircular canals, kinocilia sit on the utricular side; turning the head left deflects the cupula toward the utricle on the left (excitation) and away from the utricle on the right (inhibition), driving conjugate rightward eye movement. Key detail: Turning the head LEFT causes endolymph inertia to lag to the right, bending stereocilia TOWARD the kinocilium in the LEFT horizontal canal (DEPOLARIZING/exciting left CN VIII afferents) and AWAY from the kinocilium in the RIGHT horizontal canal (HYPERPOLARIZING/inhibiting right CN VIII afferents), driving conjugate compensatory eye rotation to the RIGHT at equal speed.

open.q: Explain how turning the head horizontally to the left alters vestibular hair cell firing in the left vs right horizontal semicircular canals and produces the vestibulo-ocular reflex.
accept: Endolymph inertia deflects stereocilia toward the kinocilium in the left horizontal canal (depolarization/excitation) and away from the kinocilium in the right horizontal canal (hyperpolarization/inhibition), driving equal-and-opposite conjugate eye movement to the right
Excites the left horizontal canal and inhibits the right horizontal canal, producing compensatory conjugate eye rotation to the right

questions.sub: Vestibular System: Semicircular Canals, Otolith Organs, and Nystagmus
questions.q: What is the 'COWS' rule for caloric vestibular testing in an awake patient (head elevated 30 degrees to align horizontal canals vertically)?
options: Cold: fast phase opposite the irrigated ear; warm: fast phase toward it (COWS)
Cold water causes pupillary dilation while warm water causes ptosis
Cold water produces fast-beating nystagmus toward the Same ear
Caloric testing evaluates the integrity of the olfactory bulb
questions.explain: Cold water sinks endolymph and inhibits the irrigated horizontal canal (eyes drift slowly toward the cold ear, triggering a fast cortical corrective saccade to the OPPOSITE side); warm water creates rising convection currents that excite the canal (fast phase to the SAME side). Key detail: Cold water irrigation produces nystagmus with its FAST phase beating to the Opposite side (slow phase toward the cold ear), whereas Warm water irrigation produces nystagmus with its FAST phase beating to the Same side (slow phase away from the warm ear).

open.q: State the direction of the slow and fast phases of nystagmus produced by cold-water versus warm-water caloric irrigation of the left ear in an awake patient.
accept: Cold water in left ear: slow vestibular drift to the left, fast corrective nystagmus beating to the right (Opposite); Warm water in left ear: slow drift to the right, fast corrective nystagmus beating to the left (Same)
Cold: slow phase same (left), fast phase opposite (right); Warm: slow phase opposite (right), fast phase same (left)

questions.sub: Gustation (Taste) and Olfaction (Smell) Transduction and Pathways
questions.q: Match the five primary taste modalities with their apical receptor transduction mechanisms on gustatory receptor cells:
options: Salty: ENaC; sour: OTOP1; sweet: T1R2/T1R3; umami: T1R1/T1R3; bitter: T2R
Sweet and bitter use direct Na+ ion channels while salty uses T2R GPCRs
All five tastes use voltage-gated K+ channels exclusively
Sour taste is mediated by T1R2+T1R3 heterodimers
questions.explain: Salty (Na+/ENaC) and sour (H+/OTOP1) depolarize taste cells directly via ion channels, whereas sweet (T1R2/T1R3), umami (T1R1/T1R3), and bitter (T2R) activate G-protein (gustducin) -> PLC-beta2 -> IP3 -> Ca2+ -> TRPM5/CALHM1 signaling. Key detail: Salty: direct Na+ influx via amiloride-sensitive ENaC channels; Sour: direct H+ influx via OTOP1 proton channels; Sweet: T1R2+T1R3 GPCR (gustducin/PLC-beta2/IP3/TRPM5); Umami: T1R1+T1R3 GPCR (L-glutamate); Bitter: T2R GPCR family (gustducin/IP3/TRPM5).

open.q: Distinguish the receptor/channel transduction mechanisms for salty, sour, sweet, umami, and bitter tastes.
accept: Salty: Na+ influx through ENaC; Sour: H+ influx through OTOP1 channels; Sweet: T1R2+T1R3 GPCR; Umami: T1R1+T1R3 GPCR; Bitter: T2R GPCRs
ENaC (salty), OTOP1 H+ channel (sour), T1R2+T1R3 GPCR (sweet), T1R1+T1R3 GPCR (umami), T2R GPCRs (bitter)

questions.sub: Gustation (Taste) and Olfaction (Smell) Transduction and Pathways
questions.q: Match the three cranial nerves carrying special sensory taste afferents from distinct regions of the tongue and pharynx to the 'nucleus tractus solitarius (NTS)':
options: Taste: anterior 2/3 CN VII; posterior 1/3 CN IX; epiglottis/pharynx CN X
Anterior 2/3: Trigeminal nerve (CN V3); Posterior 1/3: Hypoglossal nerve (CN XII); Epiglottis: Accessory nerve (CN XI)
Entire tongue taste is carried exclusively by the hypoglossal nerve (CN XII)
Anterior 2/3: CN IX; Posterior 1/3: CN VII; Epiglottis: CN V1
questions.explain: Note the key distinction on the anterior 2/3 of the tongue: CN V3 (lingual nerve) carries general somatic sensation (pain, touch, temperature), whereas CN VII (chorda tympani, hitchhiking on the lingual nerve) carries special sensory TASTE. Key detail: Anterior 2/3 of tongue: Facial nerve (CN VII via chorda tympani); Posterior 1/3 of tongue and circumvallate papillae: Glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX); Epiglottis and pharynx: Vagus nerve (CN X via internal laryngeal branch).

open.q: Name the three cranial nerves that transmit taste sensation from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue, posterior one-third of the tongue, and epiglottis/pharynx, plus their brainstem target nucleus.
accept: Anterior 2/3: Facial nerve (CN VII, chorda tympani); Posterior 1/3: Glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX); Epiglottis/pharynx: Vagus nerve (CN X); all terminate in the rostral gustatory nucleus tractus solitarius (NTS)
CN VII (anterior 2/3), CN IX (posterior 1/3), CN X (epiglottis/pharynx) -> nucleus tractus solitarius

questions.sub: Gustation (Taste) and Olfaction (Smell) Transduction and Pathways
questions.q: Trace the central ascending gustatory pathway from the nucleus tractus solitarius (NTS) to the primary gustatory cortex:
options: NTS → central tegmental tract → VPMpc thalamus → anterior insula/frontal operculum
Nucleus tractus solitarius -> lateral geniculate nucleus -> occipital lobe
Nucleus tractus solitarius -> medial geniculate nucleus -> superior temporal gyrus
Nucleus tractus solitarius -> directly to amygdala bypassing the thalamus completely
questions.explain: Unlike olfaction, taste relays through the parvocellular division of the thalamic ventral posteromedial nucleus (VPMpc) before reaching the anterior insula and frontal operculum. Key detail: Rostral gustatory nucleus tractus solitarius (NTS) -> ipsilateral central tegmental tract -> ventral posteromedial (VPMpc) nucleus of thalamus -> primary gustatory cortex (anterior insula and frontal operculum).

open.q: Name the thalamic relay nucleus and primary cortical region for conscious taste perception.
accept: Ventral posteromedial nucleus (VPM / VPMpc) of the thalamus -> anterior insula and frontal operculum
VPM nucleus of thalamus -> anterior insula / frontal operculum

questions.sub: Gustation (Taste) and Olfaction (Smell) Transduction and Pathways
questions.q: What is the intracellular signal transduction cascade in olfactory cilia when an odorant binds to an 'olfactory G-protein-coupled receptor'?
options: Odorant → Golf → adenylyl cyclase III → cAMP → cation influx → Ca2+-activated Cl− efflux
Odorant closes Na+ channels and hyperpolarizes the olfactory neuron
Odorant activates cGMP phosphodiesterase to lower cGMP
Odorant binds directly to voltage-gated K+ channels to hyperpolarize the cell
questions.explain: A unique amplifier in olfactory transduction is Ca2+-activated Cl- EFFLUX: because olfactory cilia accumulate high intracellular Cl- via NKCC1, opening Cl- channels lets negatively charged Cl- exit, boosting depolarization! Key detail: Odorant binds GPCR -> activates G-olf -> stimulates adenylyl cyclase III -> increases intracellular cAMP -> opens cAMP-gated Na+/Ca2+ channels -> Ca2+ influx opens Ca2+-activated Cl- channels (ANO2), causing Cl- EFFLUX (because olfactory cilia maintain high intracellular Cl-) and strong depolarization.

open.q: Trace the intracellular signaling cascade in olfactory receptor cilia from odorant binding to membrane depolarization, highlighting the unusual role of chloride ions.
accept: Odorant activates G-olf -> adenylyl cyclase III -> elevates cAMP -> opens cAMP-gated Na+/Ca2+ channels -> Ca2+ entry opens Ca2+-activated Cl- channels, causing depolarizing Cl- efflux (due to high intracellular Cl-)
G-olf -> adenylyl cyclase -> cAMP -> Na+/Ca2+ influx -> Ca2+-activated Cl- efflux -> depolarization

questions.sub: Gustation (Taste) and Olfaction (Smell) Transduction and Pathways
questions.q: Which unique neuroanatomical feature distinguishes the 'olfactory pathway' from vision, audition, gustation, and somatosensation?
options: Olfactory bulb output reaches piriform cortex and limbic areas without an obligatory first thalamic relay
Olfactory sensory neurons are heavily myelinated by oligodendrocytes in the nasal mucosa
Olfactory fibers cross completely in the corpus callosum before reaching the bulb
Olfaction is the only sense that projects to the spinal cord dorsal horn
questions.explain: Olfaction is the only special sense whose primary afferent pathway reaches the cerebral cortex (piriform cortex) and limbic system (amygdala/entorhinal cortex) directly without an obligatory thalamic synapse first. Key detail: Olfactory tract axons (mitral and tufted cells of the olfactory bulb) project DIRECTLY to the primary olfactory (piriform) cortex, amygdala, and entorhinal cortex WITHOUT a primary thalamic relay (only secondary projections reach the mediodorsal thalamus -> orbitofrontal cortex).

open.q: What anatomical feature makes the central olfactory pathway unique among all sensory systems regarding thalamic relay?
accept: Primary olfactory tract fibers project directly to the primary olfactory (piriform) cortex and limbic structures (amygdala, entorhinal cortex) without first relaying in the thalamus
Projects directly to the primary olfactory cortex without an obligatory thalamic relay

questions.sub: Clinical Correlations
questions.q: A 62-year-old hyperopic woman enters a dark movie theater and 30 minutes later develops sudden, severe right-sided eye pain, frontal headache, nausea/vomiting, blurred vision with rainbow-colored halos around lights, a steamy/edematous cornea, a mid-dilated (6 mm) non-reactive pupil, and a rock-hard globe (IOP 56 mmHg). What is the diagnosis and physiological mechanism?
options: Acute angle-closure glaucoma: mydriasis causes pupillary block and obstructs trabecular outflow
Primary open-angle glaucoma with normal IOP
Central retinal artery occlusion
Optic neuritis secondary to multiple sclerosis
questions.explain: Dim-light mydriasis triggers pupillary block in anatomically shallow anterior chambers, trapping aqueous humor behind the iris, bowing the iris forward over the trabecular meshwork, and causing a rapid IOP spike. Key detail: Acute angle-closure glaucoma — pupillary mydriasis in dim light caused peripheral iris crowding and pupillary block, occluding aqueous humor drainage through the trabecular meshwork and canal of Schlemm.

open.q: State the diagnosis and explain why entering a dark room precipitated acute ocular pain, halos around lights, and a fixed mid-dilated pupil.
accept: Acute angle-closure glaucoma; dim-light pupillary dilation (mydriasis) caused pupillary block and bunched the peripheral iris against the cornea, obstructing trabecular meshwork aqueous humor outflow
Acute angle-closure glaucoma; mydriasis blocked aqueous drainage at the iridocorneal angle

questions.sub: Clinical Correlations
questions.q: A 44-year-old woman reports progressive bitemporal loss of peripheral vision ('bumping into doorframes on both sides') accompanied by galactorrhea and amenorrhea. Brain MRI reveals a 2.4 cm sellar mass compressing the optic chiasm from below. Which retinal fibers are compressed?
options: Decussating nasal hemiretinal fibers from both eyes
Uncrossed temporal hemiretinal fibers from both eyes
Left optic tract fibers
Right Meyer's loop fibers
questions.explain: A prolactin-secreting pituitary macroadenoma expanding upward out of the sella turcica compresses the crossing nasal retinal fibers at the optic chiasm, abolishing both temporal visual fields (bitemporal hemianopsia).

open.q: Which retinal nerve fibers are compressed by a pituitary macroadenoma to produce bitemporal hemianopsia?
accept: Crossing (decussating) nasal hemiretinal fibers from both eyes
Nasal retinal fibers at the optic chiasm

questions.sub: Clinical Correlations
questions.q: A 71-year-old man with atrial fibrillation and carotid atherosclerosis experiences sudden, painless, complete blindness in his right eye ('like a curtain coming down'). Fundoscopy shows a diffusely pale, edematous ischemic retina with attenuated arterioles and a bright 'cherry-red spot' at the fovea. What is the diagnosis and why does the fovea appear cherry-red?
options: Central retinal artery occlusion; intact choroidal blood shines through the thin fovea
Central retinal vein occlusion (CRVO) with 'blood and thunder' hemorrhages
Wet age-related macular degeneration
Cataract
questions.explain: In CRAO, inner retinal layers opacify from ischemia, while the thin foveola (which receives oxygen from the underlying choriocapillaris rather than the central retinal artery) retains its normal red choroidal glow. Key detail: Central retinal artery occlusion (CRAO) — the thin, avascular fovea allows the intact underlying choroidal blood supply (fed by posterior ciliary arteries) to shine through against the pale infarcted inner retina.

open.q: Name the vascular occlusion causing sudden painless monocular blindness with a 'cherry-red spot' on fundoscopy and explain the anatomical basis of the cherry-red spot.
accept: Central retinal artery occlusion (CRAO); the thin foveola lacks inner retinal layers and is nourished by the underlying choroidal circulation, which shines red against the surrounding pale ischemic retina
Central retinal artery occlusion; intact choroidal perfusion shining through the thin fovea against pale ischemic retina

questions.sub: Clinical Correlations
questions.q: A 52-year-old woman presents with brief (20-30 second) episodes of severe spinning vertigo triggered specifically when rolling over in bed to her right or tilting her head back to look up, without hearing loss or tinnitus. Dix-Hallpike maneuver reproduces torsional/upbeating nystagmus after a 5-second latency. What is the pathophysiology and definitive bedside treatment?
options: BPPV: utricular otoconia enter the posterior canal; Epley manoeuvre repositions them
Meniere's disease treated with loop diuretics
Vestibular schwannoma treated with craniotomy
Acute labyrinthitis treated with systemic antibiotics
questions.explain: Free-floating utricular otoconia in the posterior semicircular canal create abnormal cupular deflection upon head position changes; the Epley maneuver guides the crystals back into the utricle. Key detail: Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV) — dislodged calcium carbonate otoconia (canaliths) from the utricle migrated into the posterior semicircular canal; treated with the Epley canalith repositioning maneuver.

open.q: State the pathophysiology and definitive bedside repositioning treatment for benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV).
accept: Dislodged utricular calcium carbonate otoconia (canaliths) enter a semicircular canal (usually the posterior canal) and deflect the cupula during head movements; treated with the Epley canalith repositioning maneuver
Displaced utricular otoconia in the posterior semicircular canal; Epley maneuver

questions.sub: Clinical Correlations
questions.q: A 46-year-old man experiences recurrent 2-hour episodes of severe rotational vertigo, a sensation of pressure/fullness in his left ear, loud roaring tinnitus, and fluctuating low-frequency sensorineural hearing loss in the left ear. What is the underlying inner ear abnormality?
options: Meniere disease: endolymphatic hydrops from impaired endolymph resorption
Otosclerosis fixing the stapes footplate
Dislodged otoconia in the superior semicircular canal
Acoustic neuroma compressing CN VII
questions.explain: Classic triad of Meniere's disease (episodic vertigo + roaring tinnitus + fluctuating low-frequency sensorineural hearing loss with aural fullness) stems from endolymphatic hydrops. Key detail: Meniere's disease — endolymphatic hydrops (increased endolymph volume and pressure distending the scala media and vestibular labyrinth due to impaired endolymphatic sac resorption).

open.q: Identify the disorder and underlying inner ear fluid disturbance in a patient with episodic vertigo, roaring tinnitus, aural fullness, and fluctuating low-frequency hearing loss.
accept: Meniere's disease; endolymphatic hydrops (excess endolymph volume/pressure in the membranous labyrinth)
Meniere's disease; endolymphatic hydrops

questions.sub: Clinical Correlations
questions.q: A 34-year-old woman in her third trimester of pregnancy develops progressive bilateral conductive hearing loss with normal tympanic membranes on otoscopy. Weber test lateralizes to the worse ear and Rinne test shows Bone Conduction > Air Conduction. Which condition causes bony ankylosis of the stapes footplate to the oval window?
options: Otosclerosis
Presbycusis
Acoustic neuroma (vestibular schwannoma)
Meniere's disease
questions.explain: Otosclerosis is an autosomal-dominant/sporadic spongy bone remodeling disorder of the otic capsule that immobilizes the stapes footplate in the oval window, frequently accelerating during pregnancy.

open.q: Name the condition that causes progressive conductive hearing loss in young adults (often worsening in pregnancy) via bony fixation of the stapes footplate.
accept: Otosclerosis

questions.sub: Clinical Correlations
questions.q: A 55-year-old man presents with progressive unilateral right-sided high-frequency sensorineural hearing loss, continuous tinnitus, and mild unsteadiness for 18 months. Brain MRI with gadolinium reveals an enhancing mass in the right cerebellopontine angle expanding the internal acoustic meatus. Which cells give rise to this tumor?
options: Schwann cells of the vestibular division of CN VIII (vestibular schwannoma / acoustic neuroma)
Oligodendrocytes of the optic chiasm
Hair cells of the Organ of Corti
Mitral cells of the olfactory bulb
questions.explain: Vestibular schwannoma (acoustic neuroma) arises from Schwann cells of the vestibular nerve within the internal acoustic meatus/cerebellopontine angle, compressing CN VIII (unilateral sensorineural deafness/tinnitus) and adjacent CN VII/CN V.

open.q: Name the most common cerebellopontine angle tumor causing progressive unilateral sensorineural hearing loss and tinnitus, and state its cell of origin.
accept: Vestibular schwannoma (acoustic neuroma); arises from Schwann cells of the vestibular division of CN VIII
Vestibular schwannoma / acoustic neuroma; Schwann cells of CN VIII

questions.sub: Clinical Correlations
questions.q: A 17-year-old boy is evaluated for delayed puberty (small testes, low LH, FSH, and testosterone) and reports that he has never been able to smell anything since childhood (congenital anosmia). What is the diagnosis and its developmental mechanism?
options: Kallmann syndrome: failed embryonic migration of GnRH neurons and olfactory axons
Pituitary apoplexy compressing the optic chiasm
Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY)
Primary hypothyroidism
questions.explain: GnRH-releasing neurons originate in the embryonic olfactory placode and migrate along olfactory axon scaffolds into the hypothalamus; ANOS1 mutations block both olfactory bulb formation (anosmia) and GnRH migration (hypogonadotropic hypogonadism). Key detail: Kallmann syndrome — failed embryonic migration of GnRH neurons and olfactory axons from the olfactory placode across the cribriform plate into the hypothalamus and olfactory bulb (often X-linked ANOS1 / KAL1 mutation).

open.q: Name the syndrome characterized by congenital anosmia and hypogonadotropic hypogonadism and explain its embryological basis.
accept: Kallmann syndrome; failure of GnRH-secreting neurons and olfactory axons to migrate together from the embryonic olfactory placode into the hypothalamus and olfactory bulb
Kallmann syndrome; defective embryonic migration of GnRH neurons and olfactory axons from the olfactory placode

questions.sub: Clinical Correlations
questions.q: A 66-year-old man with diabetes and hypertension wakes up with double vision (diplopia). On exam, his right eye is deviated 'down and out' with severe right upper lid ptosis, YET both pupils are 3 mm and constrict briskly to light. Why is the pupil spared in diabetic CN III ischemia compared with a posterior communicating artery (PCom) aneurysm?
options: Diabetes causes central CN III ischaemia; a PCom aneurysm compresses superficial parasympathetic fibres
Parasympathetic pupillary fibers travel inside the optic nerve
Diabetic neuropathy selectively destroys only the superior oblique muscle
PCom aneurysms never affect the oculomotor nerve
questions.explain: Surgical compression (PCom aneurysm, uncal herniation) hits superficial parasympathetic fibers early -> 'pupil-blown' CN III palsy; medical microvascular ischemia (diabetes, hypertension) damages central somatic motor fibers -> 'pupil-sparing' CN III palsy. Key detail: Preganglionic parasympathetic pupillomotor fibers travel superficially on the outer periphery of CN III (nourished by pial vessels, so they are compressed early by an external PCom aneurysm), whereas microvascular diabetes infarcts the central vasa nervorum core of CN III, sparing the superficial pupillary fibers.

open.q: Explain anatomically why diabetic microvascular oculomotor (CN III) palsy typically spares the pupil whereas a posterior communicating artery aneurysm causes a dilated, unreactive pupil.
accept: Superficial parasympathetic pupillomotor fibers run along the outer periphery of CN III (supplied by pial vessels), making them vulnerable to external compression by a PCom aneurysm but spared in central vasa nervorum microvascular ischemia
Parasympathetic fibers run superficially on CN III (compressed externally by aneurysms) while microvascular ischemia affects the central core

questions.sub: Clinical Correlations
questions.q: A 58-year-old man with a left posterior cerebral artery (PCA) stroke develops a right homonymous hemianopsia with 'macular sparing' (central 5-10 degrees of vision preserved). What explains macular sparing in occipital lobe infarction?
options: Macular sparing reflects dual PCA/MCA supply to the occipital pole
Macular fibers never cross in the optic chiasm
The macula is innervated by the facial nerve (CN VII)
The left optic nerve regenerates within 24 hours
questions.explain: Watershed collateral perfusion from the MCA to the occipital pole often preserves central macular vision during a PCA occlusion. Key detail: Dual arterial blood supply to the occipital pole (macular visual cortex) from both the posterior cerebral artery (PCA) and middle cerebral artery (MCA), plus a disproportionately large cortical magnification of the fovea.

open.q: Explain why a posterior cerebral artery (PCA) occipital cortex stroke often causes homonymous hemianopsia with macular sparing.
accept: The macular representation at the occipital pole receives dual collateral blood supply from both the posterior cerebral artery (PCA) and the middle cerebral artery (MCA)
Dual blood supply to the occipital pole from both the PCA and MCA

questions.sub: Clinical Correlations
questions.q: A 28-year-old woman presents with acute left-sided facial paralysis (inability to wrinkle her left forehead, close her left eye, or smile on the left), painful sensitivity to normal everyday sounds in her left ear (hyperacusis), and loss of taste on the anterior two-thirds of her left tongue. Where is the facial nerve (CN VII) lesion located?
options: Proximal facial canal (intratemporal CN VII) proximal to the branches to the stapedius muscle and chorda tympani (Bell's palsy)
Distal to the stylomastoid foramen in the parotid gland
In the right motor cortex (upper motor neuron lesion)
In the left trigeminal ganglion
questions.explain: Hyperacusis (stapedius branch) + anterior 2/3 tongue ageusia (chorda tympani) + complete ipsilateral upper/lower facial paralysis localizes CN VII injury inside the temporal bone facial canal proximal to both branches.

open.q: Localize the facial nerve (CN VII) lesion when ipsilateral upper and lower facial paralysis is accompanied by hyperacusis and loss of taste on the anterior two-thirds of the tongue.
accept: Inside the temporal bone facial canal proximal to the origin of the nerve to the stapedius and the chorda tympani
Intratemporal facial canal proximal to the stapedius and chorda tympani branches

questions.sub: Vision: Optics, Refraction, Accommodation, and Refractive Errors
questions.q: What is 'visual acuity (20/20 or 6/6 vision)' on a Snellen chart, and what minimum visual angle between two point sources can the normal human fovea resolve?
options: 20/20 (6/6) means the subject can read at 20 feet (6 meters) letters whose strokes subtend 1 minute of arc (1/60th of a degree) at the nodal point of the eye—the same distance as a standard normal observer
20/20 means the eye can only see objects within 20 inches
20/200 vision is sharper than 20/20 vision
The human fovea requires a minimum separation of 15 degrees of arc to distinguish two points
questions.explain: In 20/40 vision, a patient must stand at 20 feet to read what a normal eye reads at 40 feet; 1 arcminute corresponds to ~4.5 micrometers on the retina, matching the spacing of two adjacent foveal cones (~2-2.5 um) separated by one unstimulated cone.

open.q: Define 20/20 (6/6) Snellen visual acuity and state the minimum visual angle (in minutes of arc) resolved by the normal fovea.
accept: Ability to resolve at 20 feet (6 meters) what a normal eye resolves at 20 feet (6 meters), corresponding to a minimum separable visual angle of 1 minute of arc (1 arcminute)
Resolving at 20 ft (6 m) what a normal observer sees at 20 ft (6 m); 1 minute of arc

questions.sub: Vision: Retinal Layers, Rods vs Cones, and Phototransduction
questions.q: How does the 'trichromatic (Young-Helmholtz) theory' explain human color vision?
options: S, M and L cones peak at ~420–440, 530–535 and 560–565 nm; relative activation encodes hue
Each cone contains a rainbow prism that sorts photons mechanically by wavelength
Rods detect blue and green while cones detect only red
Humans possess 12 distinct classes of cone opsins
questions.explain: At the photoreceptor level, color is encoded trichromatically by S, M, and L cones, which retinal ganglion cells and LGN neurons subsequently recombine into red-green and blue-yellow opponent channels (Hering opponent-process theory). Key detail: Three populations of cones with overlapping absorption spectra peaking at ~420-440 nm (S-cones, blue), ~530-535 nm (M-cones, green), and ~560-565 nm (L-cones, red) encode every perceived hue by the relative ratio of their excitation levels.

open.q: Name the three cone types of human trichromatic color vision and state their approximate peak absorption wavelengths (short, medium, long).
accept: S-cones (short-wavelength/blue, ~420-440 nm), M-cones (medium-wavelength/green, ~530-535 nm), and L-cones (long-wavelength/red, ~560-565 nm)
S-cones (~420-440 nm), M-cones (~530-535 nm), and L-cones (~560-565 nm)

questions.sub: Vision: Retinal Layers, Rods vs Cones, and Phototransduction
questions.q: What are the three essential functions of the 'retinal pigment epithelium (RPE)' immediately behind the photoreceptors?
options: RPE absorbs stray light, phagocytoses shed discs, regenerates 11-cis-retinal and forms the outer blood-retinal barrier
Generates action potentials transmitted to the lateral geniculate nucleus
Secretes aqueous humor into the anterior chamber
Focuses incoming light rays by changing its curvature
questions.explain: Albinism (lack of RPE melanin) causes severe photophobia and reduced visual acuity due to internal intraocular light scatter, whereas RPE dysfunction leads to photoreceptor degeneration (e.g., dry age-related macular degeneration). Key detail: 1) Absorbs stray uncaptured photons via melanin granules to prevent internal light scatter; 2) Phagocytoses and recycles shed photoreceptor outer-segment membrane discs daily; 3) Isomerizes all-trans-retinol back into 11-cis-retinal (visual cycle) and forms the outer blood-retinal barrier.

open.q: State three physiological functions of the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE).
accept: 1) Melanin absorption of stray photons to prevent light scatter, 2) daily phagocytosis of shed photoreceptor outer-segment discs, and 3) regeneration/isomerization of 11-cis-retinal (plus forming the outer blood-retinal barrier)
Absorbs stray light via melanin, phagocytoses shed outer-segment discs, and regenerates 11-cis-retinal

questions.sub: Vision: Visual Pathways, Field Defects, and Pupillary Light Reflex
questions.q: What is 'stereopsis (binocular depth perception)', and how do 'binocular disparity-tuned neurons' in the primary visual cortex (V1) compute it?
options: Stereopsis: binocular V1 neurons compare retinal disparity to encode depth
Stereopsis depends solely on the size of the pupil in one eye
Binocular disparity occurs only when one eye is closed
Stereopsis is computed in the medial geniculate nucleus
questions.explain: Stereopsis requires overlapping binocular visual fields (central ~120 degrees) and precise ocular alignment; childhood strabismus disrupts binocular V1 column development and abolishes stereopsis (amblyopia). Key detail: Because the two eyes are separated horizontally by ~6.5 cm, slightly different 2D retinal images fall on non-corresponding points of the left and right retinas ('binocular/retinal disparity'); ocular dominance columns converge onto binocular V1 neurons tuned to specific horizontal disparities to construct 3D depth. Key detail: Retinal disparity is integrated by binocular V1 neurons to encode stereoscopic depth.

open.q: Explain the optical and cortical basis of stereopsis (true binocular 3D depth perception).
accept: Horizontal separation between the two eyes creates slight horizontal positional differences ('binocular/retinal disparity') between the left and right retinal images, which binocular neurons in primary visual cortex (V1) integrate to compute depth
Binocular retinal disparity between the two horizontally separated eyes integrated by disparity-sensitive neurons in V1

questions.sub: Audition: Tympanic Membrane, Ossicles, and Impedance Matching
questions.q: What is the 'decibel (dB) sound pressure level (SPL)' scale, and how much does sound intensity (power) increase for every +20 dB increase in sound pressure level?
options: Decibel is a logarithmic ratio scale (dB = 20 log10 [P / P0]); every +20 dB increases sound PRESSURE 10-fold and sound INTENSITY (energy) 100-fold (every +10 dB = 10-fold intensity increase)
Decibel is a linear scale where 100 dB is twice as intense as 50 dB
0 dB represents a complete vacuum with zero air molecules
Every +20 dB doubles sound intensity
questions.explain: Because human hearing spans a trillion-fold range of sound intensities (from 0 dB hearing threshold at 20 micropascals to ~120-130 dB pain threshold), sound loudness is compressed onto a logarithmic decibel scale.

open.q: State how much sound pressure and sound intensity increase for a +20 dB rise on the logarithmic decibel scale.
accept: Sound pressure increases 10-fold and sound intensity (power/energy) increases 100-fold
10-fold increase in pressure; 100-fold increase in intensity

questions.sub: Audition: Cochlear Mechanics, Organ of Corti, and Hair Cell Transduction
questions.q: What is the 'helicotrema' at the apex of the cochlea, and which two cochlear chambers communicate through it?
options: A small opening at the cochlear apex connecting the perilymph-filled SCALA VESTIBULI with the perilymph-filled SCALA TYMPANI (while the endolymph-filled scala media remains a blind-ended sealed tube)
An opening connecting the scala media with the middle ear cavity
The hole in the stapes footplate where the auditory nerve exits
A canal linking the utricle directly to the nasopharynx
questions.explain: Very low-frequency pressure waves (<20 Hz) pass lazily around the helicotrema from scala vestibuli to scala tympani without deflecting the basilar membrane, defining the lower frequency cutoff of human hearing (~20 Hz).

open.q: Identify the helicotrema and name the two cochlear fluid chambers it connects at the apex of the cochlea.
accept: An opening at the apex of the cochlea where the perilymph-filled scala vestibuli communicates directly with the perilymph-filled scala tympani
Apical cochlear opening connecting scala vestibuli and scala tympani

questions.sub: Audition: Cochlear Mechanics, Organ of Corti, and Hair Cell Transduction
questions.q: Which specialized vascular epithelium on the lateral wall of the scala media secretes K+-rich endolymph and generates the +80 mV endocochlear potential, and why do loop diuretics (furosemide, ethacrynic acid) cause ototoxicity?
options: Stria vascularis — loop diuretics inhibit its basolateral Na+-K+-2Cl- (NKCC1) cotransporter, collapsing K+ secretion and the +80 mV endocochlear potential
Tectorial membrane — loop diuretics dissolve its collagen fibers
Reissner's membrane — loop diuretics rupture the oval window
Spiral limbus — loop diuretics block acetylcholine release
questions.explain: The stria vascularis expresses the exact same NKCC1 cotransporter found in the thick ascending limb of Henle, explaining why high-dose IV loop diuretics (especially ethacrynic acid) abolish the endocochlear potential and cause acute ototoxicity.

open.q: Name the cochlear structure that secretes endolymph and generates the +80 mV endocochlear potential, and explain the mechanism of loop-diuretic ototoxicity.
accept: Stria vascularis; loop diuretics inhibit the NKCC1 cotransporter in the stria vascularis, disrupting K+ secretion and collapsing the +80 mV endocochlear potential
Stria vascularis; inhibition of its NKCC1 cotransporter reduces endolymph K+ secretion and the +80 mV potential

questions.sub: Audition: Tonotopic Organization, Auditory Pathway, and Hearing Loss Tests
questions.q: How does the 'volley principle' (phase-locking) complement 'place coding' to encode low-frequency sounds (<500-4,000 Hz) in auditory nerve fibers?
options: Phase-locked volleys across auditory fibres encode low-frequency pitch beyond single-fibre firing limits
A single auditory nerve fiber fires at 20,000 Hz continuously without a refractory period
Low frequencies are encoded solely by closing the Eustachian tube
Volley coding operates only above 18,000 Hz
questions.explain: Place coding dominates at high frequencies (>4 kHz), whereas both place coding and temporal phase-locking ('volley principle') encode low-to-mid frequencies. Key detail: Because individual spiral ganglion neurons have a refractory period limiting single-fiber firing to <1,000 Hz, groups of auditory nerve fibers fire phase-locked in alternating 'volleys' on successive cycles of a low-frequency sound wave, encoding pitch temporally alongside apical basilar membrane place coding.

open.q: Explain how the 'volley principle' enables auditory nerve fibers to encode sound frequencies higher than an individual neuron's maximum firing rate.
accept: Populations of auditory nerve fibers fire phase-locked in staggered, alternating groups ('volleys') synchronized to successive peaks of the sound wave, combining their outputs to represent the stimulus frequency
Multiple auditory neurons fire phase-locked in alternating volleys on successive sound wave cycles

questions.sub: Vestibular System: Semicircular Canals, Otolith Organs, and Nystagmus
questions.q: What is 'oculocephalic reflex (doll's eye phenomenon)' testing in an unresponsive patient, and what response indicates an intact brainstem versus brainstem dysfunction?
