options: With an intact brainstem, the eyes move opposite to head rotation; absent movement suggests impaired vestibulo-ocular pathways
With an intact brainstem, the eyes move with the head; opposite movement indicates brainstem failure
The reflex is absent in all unconscious patients, regardless of brainstem function
The test assesses the olfactory pathway and frontal cortex
questions.explain: In an awake person, cortical visual fixation suppresses the doll's eye reflex; in a comatose patient with an intact brainstem, the uninhibited VOR keeps the eyes gazing straight ahead relative to space as the head turns.

open.q: Describe the normal (intact brainstem) versus abnormal eye movement response during oculocephalic ('doll's eye') testing in a comatose patient.
accept: Intact brainstem: eyes move conjugately in the direction opposite to head rotation (preserving gaze direction); Brainstem lesion: eyes remain fixed mid-orbit and move passively with the head
Eyes deviate opposite to head turn (intact brainstem) vs eyes stay fixed with head (brainstem dysfunction)

questions.sub: Gustation (Taste) and Olfaction (Smell) Transduction and Pathways
questions.q: Match the four types of lingual papillae with their distribution on the tongue and whether they contain taste buds:
options: Circumvallate, foliate and fungiform papillae contain taste buds; filiform papillae are mechanical and lack taste buds
Filiform papillae contain most taste buds; circumvallate papillae are purely mechanical
Only fungiform papillae contain taste buds; foliate and circumvallate papillae lack them
All four papillae types contain equal numbers of taste buds
questions.explain: Mnemonic: 'Filiform = Friction only (no taste buds)', whereas Fungiform, Foliate, and Circumvallate all house taste buds.

open.q: Which lingual papillae lack taste buds and serve purely a mechanical friction role, and which papillae form a V-shaped row at the posterior tongue?
accept: Filiform papillae lack taste buds (mechanical friction only); Circumvallate papillae form the V-shaped row anterior to the sulcus terminalis
Filiform (no taste buds); circumvallate (V-shaped posterior row)

questions.sub: Gustation (Taste) and Olfaction (Smell) Transduction and Pathways
questions.q: What is 'umami' taste, which dietary molecules trigger it, and which taste receptor heterodimer mediates it?
options: Savory/meaty taste triggered by L-glutamate (e.g., monosodium glutamate, aged cheese, meat broths) and enhanced synergistically by 5'-ribonucleotides (IMP, GMP); mediated by the G-protein coupled receptor heterodimer T1R1 + T1R3
Metallic taste mediated by voltage-gated Ca2+ channels
Spicy heat sensation mediated by TRPV1 capsaicin receptors on trigeminal pain fibers
Astringent sensation mediated by sweet T1R2 receptors
questions.explain: Note that spicy 'heat' (capsaicin) and menthol 'coolness' are NOT tastes—they are chemesthetic sensations mediated by trigeminal (CN V) TRPV1 and TRPM8 somatosensory fibers!

open.q: State the primary dietary ligand and GPCR heterodimer responsible for umami taste, and identify which cranial nerve mediates spicy capsaicin sensation.
accept: L-glutamate (monosodium glutamate) binding the T1R1+T1R3 heterodimer; spicy capsaicin sensation is mediated by trigeminal nerve (CN V) TRPV1 nociceptors rather than taste buds
L-glutamate / T1R1+T1R3; trigeminal nerve (CN V) via TRPV1

questions.sub: Vision: Optics, Refraction, Accommodation, and Refractive Errors
questions.q: How do 'cataracts' impair vision, and what are the most common risk factors?
options: Lens protein opacification causes painless progressive blur, glare and loss of the red reflex
Acute painful elevation of intraocular pressure to 60 mmHg
Autoimmune demyelination of the optic chiasm
Excessive tear secretion from the lacrimal gland
questions.explain: In diabetes mellitus and galactosemia, aldose reductase converts excess glucose/galactose into osmotic sorbitol/galactitol inside lens fibers, drawing in water and causing osmotic cataract formation. Key detail: Painless, progressive opacification/clouding of the crystalline lens proteins (crystallins) causing blurred vision, glare/halos at night, and loss of red reflex; major risk factors include aging, UV-B sunlight exposure, smoking, diabetes mellitus (sorbitol accumulation via aldose reductase), and chronic corticosteroid use.

open.q: Define cataract and explain the osmotic mechanism by which diabetes mellitus accelerates cataract formation.
accept: Opacification of the crystalline lens; in diabetes, aldose reductase converts excess glucose into sorbitol inside the lens, causing osmotic water influx, lens fiber swelling, and protein opacification
Lens opacification; aldose reductase converts glucose to osmotic sorbitol causing lens swelling

questions.sub: Vision: Visual Pathways, Field Defects, and Pupillary Light Reflex
questions.q: What is 'Adie's tonic pupil' (Holmes-Adie syndrome), and how does it respond to dilute pilocarpine (0.125%)?
options: Postganglionic parasympathetic denervation causes a tonic dilated pupil that constricts to dilute pilocarpine
Sympathetic denervation causes a dilated pupil that constricts to dilute pilocarpine
Optic nerve damage causes a small pupil with brisk direct and consensual light responses
Pharmacological blockade causes a pinpoint pupil that responds strongly to dilute pilocarpine
questions.explain: Denervation supersensitivity of iris sphincter muscarinic receptors causes an Adie tonic pupil to constrict to dilute 0.125% pilocarpine (which has no effect on a normal pupil or a pharmacologically dilated pupil).

open.q: Identify the site of denervation in Adie's tonic pupil and explain why dilute 0.125% pilocarpine constricts it.
accept: Postganglionic parasympathetic neurons in the ciliary ganglion/short ciliary nerves; denervation upregulation/supersensitivity of iris sphincter muscarinic receptors causes constriction to dilute pilocarpine
Ciliary ganglion / short ciliary nerves; muscarinic denervation supersensitivity

questions.sub: Audition: Cochlear Mechanics, Organ of Corti, and Hair Cell Transduction
questions.q: What are 'Otoacoustic Emissions (OAEs)', which cells generate them, and how are they used clinically?
options: Prestin-driven outer hair-cell motility generates otoacoustic emissions, used in newborn hearing screening
Sounds produced by vocal cord vibration during snoring
Electrical spikes recorded from the primary visual cortex
Clicks generated by the temporomandibular joint
questions.explain: Because otoacoustic emissions depend on intact middle ear conduction and functioning outer hair cells, passing OAE screening rules out significant cochlear outer hair cell hearing loss in newborns. Key detail: Low-intensity acoustic sounds generated by prestin-driven electromotile contractions of healthy cochlear OUTER HAIR CELLS and measured by a sensitive microphone in the ear canal; used as a rapid, objective newborn hearing screening test (absent OAEs indicate outer hair cell or middle ear dysfunction).

open.q: Which cochlear cells generate otoacoustic emissions (OAEs) and what is their major clinical application?
accept: Outer hair cells (via prestin electromotility); universal newborn hearing screening to assess cochlear outer hair cell integrity
Outer hair cells; newborn hearing screening

questions.sub: Gustation (Taste) and Olfaction (Smell) Transduction and Pathways
questions.q: How does 'olfactory receptor combinatorial coding' allow humans with ~350-400 functional olfactory receptor genes to discriminate tens of thousands of distinct odors?
options: One receptor type per neuron; each odour activates a unique combination of olfactory glomeruli
Humans possess 100,000 different olfactory lobes in the cerebellum
Each odorant activates only a single receptor with zero overlap
Olfactory discrimination relies solely on temperature differences in nasal airflow
questions.explain: Linda Buck and Richard Axel won the 2004 Nobel Prize for discovering this 'one-neuron-one-receptor' rule and combinatorial glomerular coding in the olfactory system. Key detail: Each olfactory sensory neuron expresses only ONE olfactory receptor gene type, and all neurons expressing that receptor converge onto the same pair of glomeruli in the olfactory bulb; a single odorant molecule activates a unique combination of multiple receptor types with varying affinities, generating a distinct spatial glomerular 'odor map'.

open.q: Explain the 'one-neuron-one-receptor' rule and how combinatorial coding enables ~400 olfactory receptor types to distinguish thousands of smells.
accept: Each olfactory sensory neuron expresses only one olfactory receptor gene and projects to specific olfactory bulb glomeruli; each odorant activates a unique combination of several receptor types, creating a distinct combinatorial glomerular activation pattern
One receptor gene per neuron converging on specific glomeruli; each odor activates a unique combination of receptors

questions.sub: Clinical Correlations
questions.q: A 68-year-old man with poorly controlled diabetes mellitus and hypertension presents with sudden-onset painless vertical/diagonal diplopia that worsens when walking down stairs or reading in bed, and he unconsciously tilts his head to the LEFT to eliminate the double vision. Which cranial nerve and eye muscle are paralyzed?
options: Right Trochlear nerve (CN IV) — paralysis of the right superior oblique muscle (extorsion and depression in adduction; head tilt away from the lesion compensates via intact left superior oblique intorsion)
Left Abducens nerve (CN VI) — left lateral rectus palsy
Right Oculomotor nerve (CN III) — right medial rectus palsy
Right Optic nerve (CN II)
questions.explain: Vertical diplopia worse on looking down and inward (reading/stairs) with compensatory head tilt AWAY from the affected side (Bielschowsky head-tilt test) is pathognomonic for CN IV (superior oblique) palsy.

open.q: Identify the paralyzed cranial nerve, extraocular muscle, and side in a patient with vertical diplopia worse when walking down stairs who tilts his head to the left.
accept: Right trochlear nerve (CN IV); right superior oblique muscle
Right trochlear nerve (CN IV) / right superior oblique

questions.sub: Clinical Correlations
questions.q: A 31-year-old man sustains head trauma in a motorcycle crash and subsequently complains of clear watery fluid dripping from his right nostril when leaning forward (CSF rhinorrhea) and complete inability to smell coffee or peppermint (anosmia). Which skull base structure was fractured?
options: Cribriform plate of the ethmoid bone (shearing unmyelinated CN I olfactory fila and tearing the overlying dura/arachnoid)
Petrous temporal bone at the oval window
Greater wing of the sphenoid at the foramen ovale
Occipital condyle
questions.explain: Cribriform plate fractures tear both the delicate olfactory nerve filaments (causing anosmia) and the meningeal dural sleeves (causing CSF rhinorrhea positive for beta-2 transferrin).

open.q: Which skull base structure is fractured when head trauma causes both anosmia and CSF rhinorrhea?
accept: Cribriform plate of the ethmoid bone
Cribriform plate

questions.sub: Clinical Correlations
questions.q: A 45-year-old construction worker who worked for 20 years without ear protection around jackhammers undergoes pure-tone audiometry. His air and bone conduction thresholds are symmetric and normal from 250 Hz to 2,000 Hz, show a sharp bilateral dip ('notch') at 4,000 Hz, and partially recover at 8,000 Hz. What is the diagnosis and anatomical location of damage?
options: Noise-induced sensorineural hearing loss — destruction of stereocilia and outer/inner hair cells in the basal turn of the cochlea tuned to ~4 kHz
Conductive hearing loss from cerumen impaction
Otosclerosis of the stapes footplate
Meniere's disease affecting the cochlear apex
questions.explain: Acoustic resonance of the external auditory canal (~3-4 kHz) concentrates loud noise energy onto the basal turn of the cochlea, producing the classic 4,000 Hz audiometric notch.

open.q: Identify the diagnosis and cochlear region damaged when chronic occupational noise exposure produces a bilateral 4,000 Hz dip in both air and bone conduction.
accept: Noise-induced sensorineural hearing loss; basal turn of the cochlea (hair cells tuned to ~4 kHz)
Noise-induced sensorineural hearing loss; basal cochlea

questions.sub: Vision: Retinal Layers, Rods vs Cones, and Phototransduction
questions.q: Which vitamin is the essential dietary precursor for synthesizing the chromophore '11-cis-retinal' in both rod rhodopsin and cone iodopsins, and what is the earliest visual symptom of its deficiency?
options: Vitamin A (retinol); earliest symptom is nyctalopia (night blindness) due to impaired rod dark adaptation, progressing to xerophthalmia and Bitot spots
Vitamin C (ascorbic acid); earliest symptom is green-yellow color blindness
Vitamin D (cholecalciferol); earliest symptom is bitemporal hemianopsia
Vitamin K; earliest symptom is acute angle-closure glaucoma
questions.explain: Because rods have much lower rhodopsin regeneration efficiency and mediate scotopic night vision, Vitamin A deficiency impairs rod function first (nyctalopia).

open.q: Name the vitamin required to form 11-cis-retinal and state the earliest clinical visual symptom of its deficiency.
accept: Vitamin A (retinol); night blindness (nyctalopia)
Vitamin A; night blindness (nyctalopia)

questions.sub: Vision: Retinal Layers, Rods vs Cones, and Phototransduction
questions.q: Why does X-linked recessive 'red-green color blindness' (protanopia / deuteranopia) affect ~8% of males yet <0.5% of females?
options: The genes encoding the L-cone (red) and M-cone (green) opsins reside in tandem on the X chromosome (Xq28), making males hemizygous and prone to unequal homologous recombination/deletion, whereas the S-cone (blue) opsin gene is autosomal on chromosome 7
Females lack S-cones and L-cones entirely
The Y chromosome carries a gene that destroys red cones
Color blindness is caused by a mitochondrial mutation in the lens
questions.explain: Tandem duplication of red and green opsin genes on Xq28 predisposes to unequal crossing over during meiosis, explaining both the high prevalence and X-linked male predominance of red-green color vision defects.

open.q: Explain the chromosomal location of the red/green cone opsin genes versus the blue cone opsin gene and why red-green color blindness is much more common in males.
accept: Red (L) and green (M) opsin genes are located on the X chromosome (Xq28, X-linked recessive inheritance), so hemizygous males express the defect whenever their single X chromosome carries a mutated/deleted opsin gene; the blue (S) opsin gene is autosomal on chromosome 7
Red/green opsins are X-linked (Xq28, hemizygous in males); blue opsin is autosomal (chromosome 7)

questions.sub: Vision: Optics, Refraction, Accommodation, and Refractive Errors
questions.q: How do 'topical beta-blockers (timolol)', 'carbonic anhydrase inhibitors (acetazolamide)', 'prostaglandin F2-alpha analogs (latanoprost)', and 'muscarinic agonists (pilocarpine)' lower intraocular pressure in glaucoma?
options: Timolol and acetazolamide DECREASE aqueous humor secretion by the ciliary body epithelium; Latanoprost INCREASES uveoscleral outflow; Pilocarpine contracts the ciliary muscle to open the trabecular meshwork and INCREASES trabecular outflow
All four drugs contract the radial dilator pupillae to widen the pupil
Latanoprost increases aqueous humor secretion by 300%
Pilocarpine paralyzes the ciliary muscle (cycloplegia)
questions.explain: Glaucoma pharmacology either reduces inflow at the ciliary epithelium (beta-blockers, alpha-2 agonists, carbonic anhydrase inhibitors) or increases outflow via trabecular (pilocarpine) or uveoscleral (prostaglandin analogs) routes.

open.q: Contrast the mechanisms by which timolol/acetazolamide versus latanoprost and pilocarpine lower intraocular pressure.
accept: Timolol (beta-blocker) and acetazolamide (carbonic anhydrase inhibitor) decrease aqueous humor production by the ciliary body; latanoprost increases uveoscleral outflow; pilocarpine (M3 agonist) contracts the ciliary muscle to increase trabecular meshwork outflow
Decrease aqueous secretion (timolol/acetazolamide) vs increase uveoscleral outflow (latanoprost) and trabecular outflow (pilocarpine)

questions.sub: Vision: Visual Pathways, Field Defects, and Pupillary Light Reflex
questions.q: What is 'Anton-Babinski syndrome' (cortical blindness with visual anosognosia)?
options: Bilateral destruction of the primary visual cortices (V1, e.g., top-of-the-basilar / bilateral PCA stroke) causing complete cortical blindness WITH preserved pupillary light reflexes, accompanied by denial of blindness and confabulation of visual descriptions
Unilateral optic nerve transection with absent direct pupillary light reflex
Bilateral cataract formation with normal occipital cortex
Inability to recognize faces with intact reading
questions.explain: Intact pupillary light reflexes (mediated by subcortical pretectal pathways) in a completely blind patient who insists they can see is classic for bilateral occipital V1 infarction (Anton syndrome).

open.q: State the lesion site, status of the pupillary light reflex, and hallmark behavioral feature of Anton syndrome.
accept: Bilateral primary visual cortex (V1 / occipital lobes); pupillary light reflexes remain intact; patient denies being blind (anosognosia) and confabulates visual experiences
Bilateral occipital V1 lobes; intact pupillary light reflex; denial of blindness with confabulation

questions.sub: Audition: Cochlear Mechanics, Organ of Corti, and Hair Cell Transduction
questions.q: What is the role of the 'round window' (fenestra cochleae) at the basal end of the scala tympani?
options: Because cochlear perilymph is incompressible inside rigid bony walls, the flexible round window membrane bulges outward into the middle ear whenever the stapes footplate pushes inward at the oval window, allowing fluid pressure waves to displace the basilar membrane
The round window transmits sound waves from the cochlea directly into the cerebellum
The round window secretes endolymph into the scala media
The round window holds the malleus handle in place
questions.explain: Without a compliant pressure-relief membrane at the round window, inward movement of the stapes at the oval window could not displace incompressible perilymph along the cochlear duct.

open.q: Explain why a compliant round window membrane is mechanically essential for hearing.
accept: Because perilymph is an incompressible fluid enclosed in rigid bone, the round window bulges outward to relieve pressure each time the stapes pushes inward at the oval window, enabling traveling waves along the basilar membrane
Provides pressure relief for incompressible cochlear fluid so stapes motion can vibrate the basilar membrane

questions.sub: Vestibular System: Semicircular Canals, Otolith Organs, and Nystagmus
questions.q: What is 'motion sickness' (kinetosis), and what sensory mismatch triggers nausea, pallor, and diaphoresis?
options: Conflicting sensory signals between the vestibular labyrinth (detecting passive acceleration/roll on a boat or car) and the visual/proprioceptive systems (seeing a stationary cabin interior), activating vestibular-autonomic projections to the area postrema and medullary vomiting center
Excessive dopamine release in the substantia nigra
Occlusion of the central retinal artery
Hyperglycemia suppressing the vagus nerve
questions.explain: Antimuscarinic drugs (scopolamine patch) and H1 antihistamines (dimenhydrinate, meclizine) block cholinergic/histaminergic transmission between vestibular nuclei and the vomiting center.

open.q: Explain the sensory-conflict mechanism of motion sickness and name two receptor classes blocked by anti-motion-sickness drugs.
accept: Sensory mismatch between vestibular acceleration signals and visual/proprioceptive stability cues; blocked by muscarinic cholinergic antagonists (scopolamine) and histamine H1 antagonists (dimenhydrinate, meclizine)
Vestibular-visual sensory conflict; muscarinic (M1) and histamine (H1) receptors

questions.sub: Gustation (Taste) and Olfaction (Smell) Transduction and Pathways
questions.q: How do 'taste receptor cells' and 'olfactory sensory neurons' compare in their cellular lifespan and regenerative capacity?
options: Both continuously regenerate throughout adult life from local basal stem cells (taste bud cells turn over every ~10-14 days; olfactory receptor neurons turn over every ~30-60 days)—making them rare examples of adult neurogenesis/epithelial sensory renewal
Neither taste cells nor olfactory neurons ever divide after embryonic week 12
Taste cells live for 100 years while olfactory neurons divide every 5 minutes
Only spinal motor neurons regenerate in adults
questions.explain: Because taste cells and olfactory neurons are directly exposed to chemical toxins, heat, and pathogens in food and inspired air, continuous renewal from basal cells preserves chemosensory function (though chemotherapy or radiation transiently causes ageusia/anosmia by halting basal cell division).

open.q: State the approximate turnover time of adult taste bud receptor cells and olfactory sensory neurons and explain why chemotherapy often causes temporary loss of taste and smell.
accept: Taste cells turn over every ~10-14 days and olfactory sensory neurons every ~30-60 days from basal stem cells; chemotherapy inhibits rapidly dividing basal progenitor cells, temporarily halting receptor replacement
~10-14 days (taste) and ~30-60 days (olfactory); chemotherapy halts division of basal stem cells

questions.sub: Clinical Correlations
questions.q: A 64-year-old man with lung cancer (Pancoast tumor at the right pulmonary apex) presents with mild drooping of his right upper eyelid (ptosis), a smaller right pupil (miosis) that is most noticeable in dim lighting ('dilation lag'), and absence of sweating on the right side of his face (anhidrosis). Which neural pathway is compressed?
options: Right sympathetic chain / stellate ganglion ascending to the superior cervical ganglion (Horner syndrome)
Right oculomotor nerve (CN III)
Right optic tract
Left facial nerve (CN VII)
questions.explain: Horner syndrome (ptosis from superior tarsal muscle denervation, miosis from dilator pupillae denervation, facial anhidrosis) is caused by first-, second- (Pancoast tumor), or third-order (carotid dissection) oculosympathetic interruption.

open.q: Name the syndrome and autonomic pathway interrupted when a Pancoast lung tumor causes ipsilateral ptosis, miosis, and facial anhidrosis.
accept: Horner syndrome; ipsilateral sympathetic pathway (cervical sympathetic trunk / superior cervical ganglion)
Horner syndrome; oculosympathetic pathway

questions.sub: Clinical Correlations
questions.q: A 23-year-old woman with viral upper respiratory symptoms develops acute, continuous, severe spinning vertigo, nausea, vomiting, and spontaneous horizontal nystagmus lasting 3 days, with completely NORMAL hearing and no tinnitus. What is the diagnosis?
options: Vestibular neuronitis (acute unilateral vestibular nerve inflammation, sparing the cochlear division)
Meniere's disease
Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV)
Otosclerosis
questions.explain: Sustained severe vertigo for days WITHOUT hearing loss distinguishes vestibular neuronitis from labyrinthitis (which involves both vestibular and cochlear divisions, causing vertigo PLUS hearing loss) and BPPV (seconds-long positional episodes).

open.q: Contrast vestibular neuronitis and labyrinthitis in terms of auditory symptoms subsequent to a viral upper respiratory infection.
accept: Both cause acute sustained vertigo for days; vestibular neuronitis spares hearing (affects vestibular nerve only), whereas labyrinthitis causes both vertigo and sensorineural hearing loss/tinnitus
Hearing preserved (vestibular neuronitis) vs hearing loss/tinnitus present (labyrinthitis)

questions.sub: Clinical Correlations
questions.q: A 50-year-old man who underwent radiation therapy for nasopharyngeal carcinoma complains that all food tastes like cardboard (ageusia) and he can no longer smell his morning coffee (anosmia). Which two populations of rapidly dividing progenitor cells were damaged by radiation?
options: Lingual taste bud basal cells and nasal olfactory epithelium basal stem cells
Retinal pigment epithelial cells and lens crystallins
Spiral ganglion neurons and stria vascularis
Cerebellar granule cells and Purkinje cells
questions.explain: Radiation and cytotoxic chemotherapy arrest mitosis in rapidly cycling taste bud and olfactory basal stem cells, causing transient ageusia and anosmia until progenitor renewal resumes.

open.q: Which progenitor cell populations are damaged by head-and-neck radiotherapy to cause simultaneous loss of taste and smell?
accept: Taste bud basal cells and olfactory epithelium basal stem cells
Taste bud and olfactory basal stem cells

questions.sub: Clinical Correlations
questions.q: A 19-year-old man fails a color-vision Ishihara plate screening test during a pilot physical examination, confusing red and green numerals while identifying blue-yellow plates accurately. His maternal grandfather has the same condition. Which photoreceptors are defective and where is the mutated gene located?
options: L-cones (red) or M-cones (green); X chromosome (Xq28, X-linked recessive inheritance)
S-cones (blue); chromosome 7
Peripheral rods; chromosome 21
Intrinsically photosensitive melanopsin ganglion cells; mitochondrial DNA
questions.explain: X-linked recessive inheritance (affected maternal grandfather -> carrier mother -> affected grandson) with red-green confusion localizes to L or M cone opsin genes on Xq28.

open.q: State the defective cone types and chromosomal inheritance pattern in classic red-green color blindness.
accept: L-cones (red) or M-cones (green); X-linked recessive inheritance (Xq28)
L/M cones; X-linked recessive

questions.sub: Clinical Correlations
questions.q: A 57-year-old man has a right parietal lobe stroke damaging the superior optic radiations (Baum's loop). Which visual field quadrant is lost on formal perimetry?
options: Left inferior homonymous quadrantanopia ('pie on the floor')
Left superior homonymous quadrantanopia ('pie in the sky')
Bitemporal hemianopsia
Right monocular blindness
questions.explain: Superior optic radiations pass through the parietal lobe (representing the superior retina = inferior visual field), so a right parietal lesion produces a contralateral (left) inferior quadrantanopia.

open.q: State the visual field defect caused by damage to the right parietal superior optic radiations (Baum's loop).
accept: Left inferior homonymous quadrantanopia ('pie on the floor')
Left inferior homonymous quadrantanopia

questions.sub: Vision: Optics, Refraction, Accommodation, and Refractive Errors
questions.q: What is the 'blind spot (Mariotte's spot)' in the visual field, and why are we normally unaware of it during everyday monocular or binocular vision?
options: The optic disc creates a temporal visual-field scotoma, masked by fellow-eye overlap and cortical fill-in
A blind area directly in the center of the fovea caused by blood vessels
An area of complete blindness covering the entire upper visual field
A region of the cornea lacking epithelial cells
questions.explain: Because the optic disc lies ~15 degrees nasal to the fovea on the retina, optical inversion projects the physiological blind spot ~15 degrees temporal to fixation in each eye's visual field. Key detail: A physiological scotoma ~15 degrees temporal to the point of fixation corresponding to the photoreceptor-free optic disc (nasal retina); we do not notice it because the opposite eye's visual field overlaps it during binocular viewing AND the visual cortex perceptually 'fills in' the gap using surrounding surface patterns.

open.q: State the anatomical location of the physiological blind spot on the retina, its position in the visual field relative to fixation, and why it goes unnoticed.
accept: Optic disc (located nasal to the fovea); projects ~15 degrees temporal to fixation in the visual field; unnoticed due to binocular overlap from the fellow eye and cortical perceptual filling-in
Optic disc (~15 degrees temporal in visual field); masked by binocular overlap and cortical filling-in

questions.sub: Vision: Retinal Layers, Rods vs Cones, and Phototransduction
questions.q: How does 'light adaptation' adjust retinal sensitivity when stepping from a dark theater into bright noon sunlight?
options: Bright light reduces photoreceptor cGMP and closes cation channels; calcium-dependent feedback adjusts sensitivity to prevent saturation
Bright light raises cGMP and keeps all cation channels open, increasing dark current
Light adaptation occurs by permanently destroying cone and rod photopigments
Bright light increases photoreceptor calcium and suppresses guanylyl cyclase
questions.explain: Intracellular Ca2+ feedback via guanylyl cyclase-activating proteins (GCAPs) and recoverin prevents photoreceptors from saturating across a 10-billion-fold range of ambient illumination.

open.q: Explain the intracellular role of decreased photoreceptor Ca2+ during light adaptation in bright sunlight.
accept: Closure of CNG channels lowers intracellular Ca2+, which activates guanylyl cyclase (via GCAPs) to replenish cGMP and adjusts channel/rhodopsin sensitivity so photoreceptors avoid saturation in bright light
Lower intracellular Ca2+ stimulates guanylyl cyclase to restore cGMP and recalibrate sensitivity without saturation

questions.sub: Vision: Visual Pathways, Field Defects, and Pupillary Light Reflex
questions.q: What is 'blindsight' following unilateral destruction of the primary visual cortex (V1)?
options: V1 damage causes conscious field blindness but preserves unconscious subcortical visual guidance
Ability to see in total darkness without any photons
Complete restoration of 20/10 reading acuity after bilateral occipital removal
Ability to hear colors through the medial geniculate nucleus
questions.explain: Blindsight demonstrates that subcortical retinotectal (superior colliculus -> pulvinar -> extrastriate motion cortex) pathways guide unconscious visuomotor localization even when conscious V1 perception is lost. Key detail: Patients report complete conscious blindness in the contralateral hemifield, yet can accurately point to, reach for, or guess the direction of moving stimuli presented in their blind hemifield via intact subcortical projections from the retina to the superior colliculus and pulvinar -> extrastriate visual cortex (V5/MT).

open.q: Define blindsight and name the subcortical visual pathway that mediates unconscious visuomotor localization when primary visual cortex (V1) is destroyed.
accept: Ability of patients with V1 lesions to unconsciously localize or detect motion in their blind visual field without conscious visual awareness; mediated by the retinotectal pathway (retina -> superior colliculus -> pulvinar -> extrastriate cortex)
Unconscious visuomotor localization in a cortically blind field via the superior colliculus-pulvinar-extrastriate pathway

questions.sub: Audition: Tympanic Membrane, Ossicles, and Impedance Matching
questions.q: Compare 'air conduction' and 'bone conduction' of sound to the cochlea:
options: Air conduction uses the tympanic membrane/ossicles; bone conduction transmits skull vibration directly to the cochlea
Bone conduction is normally three times louder than air conduction in healthy ears
Air conduction bypasses the tympanic membrane and ossicles completely
Bone conduction requires an intact stapes footplate to vibrate
questions.explain: Because bone conduction bypasses the external ear canal, tympanic membrane, and ossicles, preserved bone conduction with reduced air conduction (Rinne negative, BC > AC) diagnoses conductive hearing loss. Key detail: Air conduction (normally ~2x more sensitive/longer-lasting than bone conduction) transmits airborne sound waves via the pinna, external auditory canal, tympanic membrane, and ossicular chain to the oval window; Bone conduction transmits skull vibrations directly through the temporal bone to the cochlea, bypassing the external and middle ear.

open.q: Explain why bone conduction remains intact while air conduction is reduced in conductive hearing loss.
accept: Bone conduction transmits vibrations directly through the skull bone to the inner ear cochlea, bypassing the external auditory canal, tympanic membrane, and middle ear ossicles
Bone conduction vibrates the cochlea directly through the skull, bypassing the external and middle ear

questions.sub: Audition: Cochlear Mechanics, Organ of Corti, and Hair Cell Transduction
questions.q: How do 'tip links' and 'myosin motors' in cochlear hair cell stereocilia maintain optimal mechanotransduction sensitivity ('adaptation')?
options: Tip links gate MET channels; Ca2+-dependent myosin adaptation resets their tension
Tip links are myelinated axons that conduct action potentials to the brainstem
Myosin motors contract the tympanic membrane
Tip links dissolve permanently after every single sound wave
questions.explain: Fast Ca2+-dependent myosin adaptation resets the resting tension of stereociliary tip links within milliseconds so hair cells can track vibrations up to 20,000 Hz. Key detail: Cadherin-23/protocadherin-15 tip links connect shorter stereocilia to taller adjacent stereocilia; during sustained deflection, Ca2+ influx through open MET channels triggers myosin-1c/VIIa motors to slip down the actin core, relaxing tip-link tension so the channel can respond to new high-frequency oscillations.

open.q: Describe the structural role of stereociliary 'tip links' in hair cell mechanotransduction.
accept: Tip links are protein filaments connecting the tip of each shorter stereocilium to the side of its taller neighbor; bending stereocilia toward the tallest stereocilium tenses the tip links and mechanically pulls open mechanoelectrical transduction (MET) cation channels
Filaments linking adjacent stereocilia that pull open MET ion channels when stereocilia bend toward the tallest stereocilium

questions.sub: Audition: Tonotopic Organization, Auditory Pathway, and Hearing Loss Tests
questions.q: What is 'presbycusis' (age-related sensorineural hearing loss), and which frequencies are lost first?
options: Symmetric, progressive, bilateral HIGH-FREQUENCY sensorineural hearing loss (typically >2,000-4,000 Hz, impairing consonant discrimination in noisy environments) caused by cumulative degeneration of hair cells, spiral ganglion neurons, and stria vascularis in the basal turn of the cochlea
Unilateral low-frequency conductive hearing loss caused by earwax
Sudden complete deafness in the left ear at age 12
Excessive sensitivity to ultrasound above 50,000 Hz
questions.explain: Because high-frequency consonants (s, f, t, k, sh) carry speech intelligibility while low-frequency vowels carry volume, presbycusis patients often say 'I can hear people talking, I just can't make out the words.'

open.q: Define presbycusis, identify which sound frequencies are affected earliest, and name the cochlear region that degenerates first.
accept: Progressive bilateral age-related sensorineural hearing loss; high frequencies are lost earliest due to degeneration of hair cells and spiral ganglion neurons in the basal turn of the cochlea
Age-related sensorineural hearing loss; high frequencies lost first due to basal cochlear degeneration

questions.sub: Vestibular System: Semicircular Canals, Otolith Organs, and Nystagmus
questions.q: What is 'vestibular compensation' following an acute unilateral labyrinthine lesion (e.g., vestibular neuronitis or labyrinthectomy)?
options: Within days to weeks, central brainstem vestibular nuclei and the vestibulocerebellum rebalance resting tonic firing rates between the intact and deafferented sides, resolving spontaneous nystagmus and severe vertigo at rest even though the peripheral labyrinth remains damaged
The damaged semicircular canal grows back completely within 48 hours
The optic nerve takes over sensing angular head rotation
Vertigo persists at full intensity for 50 years without any improvement
questions.explain: Because vestibular compensation relies on active cerebellar and brainstem recalibration, prolonged use of vestibular suppressants (meclizine, benzodiazepines) beyond the first 48-72 hours delays central recovery!

open.q: Explain how central vestibular compensation resolves spontaneous vertigo after unilateral vestibular loss and why prolonged vestibular-suppressant medication should be avoided.
accept: Brainstem vestibular nuclei and the cerebellum recalibrate tonic resting discharge rates between the two sides to restore balance; prolonged vestibular-suppressant drugs blunt the error signals needed for central neuroplastic compensation and delay recovery
Cerebellar/brainstem rebalancing of tonic vestibular firing; prolonged suppressants impair central compensation

questions.sub: Gustation (Taste) and Olfaction (Smell) Transduction and Pathways
questions.q: How do 'retronasal olfaction' and 'gustation' combine to produce the perception of food 'flavor'?
options: Retronasal aroma combines with taste and trigeminal input to create flavour
Taste buds on the tongue detect 10,000 different volatile aromas directly
The Eustachian tube carries food particles to the olfactory bulb
Flavor is processed exclusively in the spinal dorsal horn
questions.explain: What patients call 'loss of taste' during viral rhinitis or COVID-19 is almost always loss of retronasal olfaction (anosmia), while true sweet/salty/sour/bitter/umami tongue sensation remains intact. Key detail: Volatile aroma molecules released from warm food in the mouth travel upward behind the soft palate through the nasopharynx to stimulate the olfactory epithelium (retronasal olfaction), integrating with gustatory (taste) and trigeminal texture/temperature inputs in the orbitofrontal cortex—which is why a nasal cold makes food seem 'tasteless'.

open.q: Explain why patients with nasal congestion or viral anosmia report that food 'has no taste' even when their lingual taste buds are intact.
accept: Most of food 'flavor' comes from volatile food aromas traveling from the mouth through the nasopharynx to the olfactory epithelium (retronasal olfaction); blocking airflow or damaging olfactory neurons eliminates retronasal aroma input
Loss of retronasal olfaction (aroma molecules reaching the olfactory epithelium from the nasopharynx), which normally combines with basic taste to create flavor

questions.sub: Clinical Correlations
questions.q: A 66-year-old man with hypertension and diabetes presents with sudden painless monocular vision loss in his right eye after waking up. Fundoscopy reveals severe retinal venous engorgement and tortuosity, diffuse four-quadrant retinal hemorrhages ('blood and thunder' appearance), cotton-wool spots, and optic disc edema. What is the diagnosis?
options: Central retinal vein occlusion (CRVO)
Central retinal artery occlusion (CRAO)
Cataract
Horner syndrome
questions.explain: Dilated tortuous veins + diffuse four-quadrant hemorrhages ('blood and thunder' fundus) = CRVO, whereas pale ischemic retina + cherry-red foveal spot = CRAO.

open.q: Name the retinal vascular occlusion that produces a 'blood and thunder' fundus with dilated tortuous veins and four-quadrant hemorrhages.
accept: Central retinal vein occlusion (CRVO)
Central retinal vein occlusion

questions.sub: Clinical Correlations
questions.q: A 42-year-old woman with high myopia notices a sudden shower of new floaters and flashing lights (photopsias) in her left eye, followed hours later by a dark 'curtain' descending over her upper visual field. What ophthalmic emergency has occurred?
options: Rhegmatogenous retinal detachment (separation of the neurosensory retina from the underlying retinal pigment epithelium)
Bacterial conjunctivitis
Presbyopia
Arcus senilis
questions.explain: Flashes (vitreous traction on retina) + sudden floaters + a progressive dark curtain/shadow indicate retinal detachment, requiring urgent surgical reattachment before the macula detaches.

open.q: Identify the ophthalmic emergency signaled by sudden flashes of light, floaters, and a dark curtain moving across the visual field, and name the two retinal layers that separate.
accept: Retinal detachment; separation of the neurosensory retina (photoreceptor layer) from the underlying retinal pigment epithelium (RPE)
Retinal detachment; neurosensory retina separates from the retinal pigment epithelium

questions.sub: Clinical Correlations
questions.q: A 35-year-old man is diagnosed with severe open-angle glaucoma and is prescribed topical latanoprost eye drops once nightly. After 6 months, his intraocular pressure is well controlled at 14 mmHg, and he notices his blue-hazel iris has gradually darkened to brown and his eyelashes have grown longer and thicker. How did latanoprost lower his IOP?
options: As a prostaglandin F2-alpha analog, it relaxes ciliary muscle bundles and remodels extracellular matrix to INCREASE uveoscleral outflow of aqueous humor
It blocks carbonic anhydrase in the choroid plexus
It constricts the pupil via muscarinic M3 agonism
It blocks beta-1 receptors on the sinoatrial node
questions.explain: Prostaglandin analogs (latanoprost, bimatoprost) are first-line topical agents for open-angle glaucoma because they potently increase uveoscleral outflow with once-daily dosing (causing harmless iris hyperpigmentation and lash hypertrichosis).

open.q: State the drug class and aqueous-humor drainage mechanism of latanoprost in open-angle glaucoma.
accept: Prostaglandin F2-alpha analog; increases uveoscleral outflow of aqueous humor
Prostaglandin analog; increases uveoscleral outflow

questions.sub: Clinical Correlations
questions.q: A 6-year-old boy presents with muffled hearing in his right ear for 2 months without fever or severe ear pain. Otoscopy shows a dull, amber-colored, retracted tympanic membrane with visible air-fluid bubbles and reduced mobility on pneumatic otoscopy. Weber test lateralizes to the right ear and Rinne test shows BC > AC on the right. What is the diagnosis?
options: Otitis media with effusion (serous otitis media) causing conductive hearing loss due to Eustachian tube dysfunction
Bilateral sensorineural presbycusis
Acoustic neuroma
Meniere's disease
questions.explain: Eustachian tube obstruction (often from adenoidal hypertrophy) creates negative middle ear pressure and sterile serous fluid accumulation that dampens tympanic membrane/ossicular vibration (conductive hearing loss).

open.q: Identify the middle ear condition causing painless conductive hearing loss with a retracted amber tympanic membrane and fluid levels in a child.
accept: Otitis media with effusion (serous otitis media)
Otitis media with effusion

questions.sub: Clinical Correlations
questions.q: A 29-year-old woman sustains a longitudinal temporal bone fracture after a motor vehicle collision and develops conductive hearing loss in her left ear with intact facial nerve function and a hemotympanum. Tympanometry shows a hypercompliant ('Ad') peak. What middle ear injury occurred?
options: Ossicular chain discontinuity (dislocation of the incudostapedial joint)
Stapes footplate fixation (otosclerosis)
Complete transection of the brainstem lateral lemniscus
Rupture of the round window into the cerebellum
questions.explain: Ossicular chain disruption breaks the mechanical lever between the tympanic membrane and oval window, causing a large (~50-60 dB) conductive hearing loss and an abnormally floppy/hypercompliant tympanogram.

open.q: What middle ear mechanical injury causes severe conductive hearing loss with an abnormally hypercompliant tympanic membrane after temporal bone trauma?
accept: Ossicular chain discontinuity / dislocation
Ossicular chain disruption

questions.sub: Clinical Correlations
questions.q: A 54-year-old man undergoes middle ear surgery (stapedectomy) during which the chorda tympani nerve is inadvertently stretched as it crosses the medial surface of the tympanic membrane between the malleus and incus. What postoperative sensory deficit will he notice?
options: Loss of taste sensation on the ipsilateral anterior two-thirds of the tongue (along with reduced submandibular/sublingual salivation)
Complete paralysis of tongue protrusion
Loss of pain and temperature on the anterior two-thirds of the tongue
Bilateral anosmia
questions.explain: The chorda tympani (branch of CN VII) runs right across the middle ear cavity between the malleus and incus, carrying special sensory taste from the anterior 2/3 of the tongue and parasympathetic fibers to the submandibular ganglion.

open.q: State the sensory deficit produced by injury to the chorda tympani nerve inside the middle ear cavity.
accept: Loss of taste (ageusia) on the ipsilateral anterior two-thirds of the tongue
Loss of taste on the ipsilateral anterior two-thirds of the tongue

questions.sub: Clinical Correlations
questions.q: A 70-year-old man with early Alzheimer's disease or Parkinson's disease is evaluated because he has progressively lost his sense of smell (hyposmia/anosmia) over the past 4 years, well before developing overt memory or motor symptoms. Which olfactory structure accumulates tau/alpha-synuclein pathology early in these neurodegenerative diseases?
options: Olfactory bulb and anterior olfactory nucleus / entorhinal cortex
Cochlear stria vascularis
Tympanic membrane
Superior oblique muscle
questions.explain: Early degeneration of the olfactory bulb and entorhinal/piriform olfactory cortex makes unexplained hyposmia a classic prodromal biomarker of both Parkinson's disease and Alzheimer's disease.

open.q: Which chemosensory deficit frequently precedes overt motor or cognitive symptoms by years in Parkinson's disease and Alzheimer's disease?
accept: Hyposmia / anosmia (loss of smell) due to early pathology in the olfactory bulb and entorhinal/olfactory cortex
Hyposmia / anosmia (impaired olfaction)

questions.sub: Clinical Correlations
questions.q: A 65-year-old man is brought to the emergency department comatose after a brainstem hemorrhage. When the physician irrigates his right external auditory canal with ice-cold water, BOTH eyes deviate slowly and conjugately to the RIGHT and remain stuck looking right without any fast corrective beat back to the left. What does this tell you about his brainstem versus cerebral cortex?
options: Cold calorics cause slow eye deviation toward the irrigated ear; absent fast phase suggests cortical coma with intact brainstem VOR
His entire brainstem is completely dead
He is awake and feigning coma
His right optic nerve is transected
questions.explain: Tonic conjugate eye deviation toward cold water without a fast corrective phase confirms intact brainstem oculomotor/vestibular circuitry alongside diffuse cortical coma. Key detail: His brainstem VOR pathways (CN VIII -> vestibular nuclei -> PPRF/MLF -> CN VI & CN III) are INTACT (producing the tonic slow drift toward the cold-irrigated ear), whereas his cerebral cortex/frontal eye fields are suppressed by coma (eliminating the fast cortical corrective saccade).

open.q: Interpret the finding when cold caloric irrigation of the right ear in a comatose patient produces tonic conjugate eye deviation to the right without a fast corrective nystagmus phase.
accept: Brainstem vestibulo-ocular reflex pathways are intact (slow drift toward the cold ear), while cortical function is suppressed (absent fast corrective saccade)
Intact brainstem VOR pathways with suppressed cortical function

questions.sub: Vision: Optics, Refraction, Accommodation, and Refractive Errors
questions.q: Which ocular structures form the 'blood-aqueous barrier' and 'blood-retinal barrier' to keep the optical media crystal clear and immune-privileged?
options: Tight junctions between non-pigmented ciliary body epithelial cells and iris capillary endothelium (blood-aqueous barrier), plus tight junctions between retinal capillary endothelial cells and retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells (blood-retinal barrier)
Fenestrated capillaries of the conjunctiva
Sweat glands of the eyelid
Tendons of the extraocular muscles
questions.explain: Tight junctions in the ciliary epithelium, retinal capillary endothelium, and RPE prevent plasma proteins and leukocytes from clouding the aqueous humor, vitreous humor, and retina.

open.q: Name the two cellular barriers that maintain the optical clarity and immune privilege of the eye.
accept: Blood-aqueous barrier (non-pigmented ciliary epithelium & iris capillary tight junctions) and blood-retinal barrier (retinal capillary endothelium & retinal pigment epithelium tight junctions)
Blood-aqueous barrier and blood-retinal barrier

questions.sub: Vision: Visual Pathways, Field Defects, and Pupillary Light Reflex
questions.q: What is 'hemianopic macular splitting' versus 'macular sparing', and why does a lesion of the right optic tract cause macular splitting whereas a right PCA occipital infarct often shows macular sparing?
options: Optic tract lesions split the macula; dual PCA/MCA supply to the occipital pole can spare it
The optic tract contains only rod axons from the far periphery
Macular fibers cross twice in the corpus callosum
The occipital lobe has zero blood vessels
questions.explain: Macular sparing is a hallmark localizing feature of occipital cortical (PCA) strokes versus optic tract or LGN lesions. Key detail: In the optic tract, macular and peripheral fibers from the left visual hemifield run tightly intermingled without dual blood supply (so a tract lesion splits the macula cleanly down the vertical midline); in the occipital cortex, the large macular representation at the occipital pole receives dual perfusion from both the PCA and MCA.

open.q: Explain why an optic tract lesion causes macular splitting whereas a Posterior Cerebral Artery occipital stroke commonly exhibits macular sparing.
accept: Optic tract fibers lack collateral dual perfusion so a lesion affects both macular and peripheral hemifield fibers equally, whereas the occipital pole (macular cortex) receives dual blood supply from both the PCA and MCA
No dual blood supply in the optic tract vs dual PCA/MCA collateral perfusion at the occipital pole

questions.sub: Audition: Cochlear Mechanics, Organ of Corti, and Hair Cell Transduction
questions.q: How do 'auditory brainstem response (ABR / BAER)' evoked potentials clinically evaluate hearing and brainstem integrity in infants or comatose patients?
options: ABR records short-latency scalp potentials after clicks; successive waves reflect activity from CN VIII through the auditory brainstem to the inferior colliculus
ABR records retinal responses to flashes and localises lesions in the optic tract
ABR measures cochlear hair-cell movement using tympanic membrane pressure
ABR records cortical slow waves during sleep and cannot assess brainstem pathways
questions.explain: ABR waves I-V map directly onto the brainstem auditory pathway (CN VIII -> Cochlear nucleus -> Superior olive -> Lateral lemniscus -> Inferior colliculus) to detect newborn sensorineural deafness or vestibular schwannoma conduction delay.

open.q: Match Waves I, III, and V of the Auditory Brainstem Response (ABR) with their corresponding anatomical generators.
accept: Wave I: auditory nerve (CN VIII); Wave III: superior olivary complex; Wave V: inferior colliculus
CN VIII (Wave I), superior olivary complex (Wave III), inferior colliculus (Wave V)

questions.sub: Vestibular System: Semicircular Canals, Otolith Organs, and Nystagmus
questions.q: How is the direction of 'nystagmus' named clinically (e.g., 'right-beating nystagmus'), and which phase is the pathological vestibular drift versus the brainstem/cortical corrective reset?
options: Nystagmus is named by the direction of its FAST corrective saccadic phase; the SLOW phase is the primary pathological vestibular drift (usually toward the hypofunctioning labyrinth), while the FAST phase is the rapid corrective snap back in the opposite direction
Nystagmus is named by the slow phase; the fast phase occurs only during deep sleep
Both slow and fast phases move in the exact same direction continuously
Nystagmus is caused by contraction of the stapedius muscle
questions.explain: In acute left vestibular neuronitis, impaired left vestibular tone allows the intact right labyrinth to push the eyes slowly to the LEFT (slow phase), triggering a fast corrective beat to the RIGHT ('right-beating nystagmus' away from the lesioned ear).

open.q: State which phase (slow vs fast) gives nystagmus its clinical name and explain which phase represents the primary vestibular drift versus the corrective reset.
accept: Named by the direction of the fast phase; the slow phase is the primary vestibular drift (toward the weaker labyrinth), and the fast phase is the rapid corrective reset in the opposite direction
Named by the fast phase; slow phase = vestibular drift, fast phase = corrective saccade

questions.sub: Clinical Correlations
questions.q: A 40-year-old woman presents with progressive bilateral vision loss starting as night blindness (nyctalopia) in adolescence and advancing to severe peripheral 'tunnel vision,' while central reading acuity remained preserved until recently. Fundoscopy reveals bone-spicule pigment deposits in the mid-peripheral retina, attenuated arterioles, and waxy optic disc pallor. What is the diagnosis?
options: Retinitis pigmentosa (inherited progressive degeneration of rod photoreceptors followed by cones)
Age-related macular degeneration
Central retinal artery occlusion
Acute angle-closure glaucoma
questions.explain: Night blindness + progressive peripheral tunnel vision + bone-spicule retinal pigmentation is diagnostic of retinitis pigmentosa (primary rod degeneration).

open.q: Name the inherited retinal dystrophy characterized by early night blindness, progressive peripheral tunnel vision, and bone-spicule retinal pigmentation.
accept: Retinitis pigmentosa

questions.sub: Clinical Correlations
questions.q: A 69-year-old man who underwent bilateral cataract surgery years ago develops sudden painless vision loss in his right eye after a minor fall. On examination, he has a superotemporal visual field defect and a shimmering grey membrane billowing inside the vitreous cavity on fundoscopy. Why does pseudophakia (prior cataract surgery) increase the risk of retinal detachment?
options: Cataract extraction accelerates posterior vitreous detachment and vitreous liquefaction, increasing tractional tears in the peripheral neurosensory retina that allow liquefied vitreous to dissect beneath the retina
Cataract surgery destroys the optic chiasm
Artificial intraocular lenses secrete hydrochloric acid
Cataract surgery causes acute angle-closure glaucoma in 90% of patients
questions.explain: High myopia, prior intraocular surgery (cataract extraction), and ocular trauma are the three classic risk factors for rhegmatogenous retinal detachment.

open.q: List three major clinical risk factors for rhegmatogenous retinal detachment.
accept: High myopia (nearsightedness), prior cataract/intraocular surgery, and ocular trauma
High myopia, prior cataract surgery, and eye trauma

questions.sub: Clinical Correlations
questions.q: A 55-year-old man with chronic open-angle glaucoma is accidentally given tropicamide (a muscarinic antagonist mydriatic) eye drops before a routine dilated fundus exam, and within 45 minutes develops excruciating eye pain, corneal clouding, nausea, and IOP of 52 mmHg. Why did tropicamide precipitate this crisis?
options: Muscarinic M3 blockade paralyzed the iris sphincter pupillae, causing mydriasis that crowded the peripheral iris into an anatomically narrow iridocorneal angle and blocked trabecular aqueous drainage
Tropicamide constricted the pupil to 0.5 mm
Tropicamide caused central retinal artery embolism
Tropicamide paralyzed the lateral rectus muscle
questions.explain: Anticholinergic mydriatics (tropicamide, atropine) and sympathomimetic alpha-1 agonists (phenylephrine) can precipitate acute angle-closure glaucoma in patients with anatomically shallow anterior chambers.

open.q: Explain why anticholinergic mydriatic drops (e.g., tropicamide) can trigger acute angle-closure glaucoma in predisposed eyes.
accept: Pupillary dilation (mydriasis) bunches the peripheral iris into the iridocorneal angle, mechanically blocking aqueous humor outflow through the trabecular meshwork and canal of Schlemm
Mydriasis crowds the peripheral iris against the trabecular meshwork, blocking aqueous drainage

questions.sub: Clinical Correlations
questions.q: A 22-year-old woman presents with a 3-day history of painful blurred vision in her left eye (worse when moving the eye), washed-out red color perception ('red desaturation'), and a left Relative Afferent Pupillary Defect (RAPD). Fundoscopy is completely normal ('the doctor sees nothing and the patient sees nothing'). What is the diagnosis?
options: Retrobulbar optic neuritis (strongly associated with multiple sclerosis)
Cataract
Central retinal vein occlusion
Presbyopia
questions.explain: Painful monocular vision loss + red color desaturation + RAPD + normal optic disc appearance ('retrobulbar' inflammation posterior to the lamina cribrosa) is classic for MS-associated optic neuritis.

open.q: State the diagnosis when a young adult develops painful monocular vision loss, red color desaturation, a relative afferent pupillary defect, and a normal-appearing optic disc.
accept: Retrobulbar optic neuritis (often associated with multiple sclerosis)
Retrobulbar optic neuritis

questions.sub: Clinical Correlations
questions.q: A 38-year-old man is struck on the side of the head by a baseball and develops immediate left-sided hearing loss and vertigo, with blood draining from the left external auditory canal and a facial nerve palsy. Rinne test on the left shows Air Conduction > Bone Conduction, and Weber lateralizes to the right ear. What type of temporal bone fracture occurred?
options: Transverse temporal bone fracture
Longitudinal temporal bone fracture
Transverse occipital bone fracture
Longitudinal occipital bone fracture
questions.explain: Longitudinal temporal bone fractures (80%) run parallel to the petrous ridge and disrupt the ossicles/tympanic membrane (conductive hearing loss), whereas transverse fractures (20%) cut across the petrous pyramid and otic capsule (sensorineural hearing loss, vertigo, and frequent CN VII injury).

open.q: Contrast longitudinal versus transverse temporal bone fractures in terms of hearing loss type (conductive vs sensorineural).
accept: Longitudinal fracture: disrupts the middle ear ossicles/tympanic membrane -> conductive hearing loss; Transverse fracture: cuts across the otic capsule/cochlea/CN VIII -> sensorineural hearing loss (and vertigo/CN VII palsy)
Conductive hearing loss (longitudinal) vs sensorineural hearing loss (transverse)

questions.sub: Clinical Correlations
questions.q: A 61-year-old man develops sudden-onset severe vertigo, dysphagia, hoarseness, ipsilateral left facial loss of pain/temperature, contralateral right body loss of pain/temperature, left limb ataxia, and left Horner syndrome. Which vestibular structure is infarcted to cause his severe vertigo and nystagmus?
options: Left vestibular nuclei in the lateral medulla (Wallenberg lateral medullary syndrome from left PICA or vertebral artery occlusion)
Left cochlear stria vascularis
Right superior colliculus
Bilateral olfactory bulbs
questions.explain: Vertigo, nausea, vomiting, and nystagmus are hallmark symptoms of lateral medullary (Wallenberg) infarction due to damage to the vestibular nuclei.

open.q: Which brainstem sensory nuclei are damaged in Wallenberg lateral medullary syndrome to produce acute severe vertigo, nausea, and nystagmus?
accept: Vestibular nuclei

questions.sub: Clinical Correlations
questions.q: A 30-year-old woman complains of a metallic/sour taste disturbance (dysgeusia) and dry mouth after starting an ACE inhibitor (captopril) and zinc deficiency. Which ions normally depolarize sour and salty taste receptor cells?
options: H+ (protons via OTOP1 channels) for sour taste, and Na+ (via ENaC channels) for salty taste
Cl- and HCO3- for sweet taste
Ca2+ and Mg2+ for bitter taste
Fe2+ for umami taste
questions.explain: Sour transduction depends on H+ influx through OTOP1 proton channels, while salty transduction depends on Na+ influx through amiloride-sensitive ENaC channels.

open.q: Name the specific ions and apical channels responsible for sour and salty taste transduction.
accept: Sour: H+ ions entering via OTOP1 proton channels; Salty: Na+ ions entering via epithelial Na+ channels (ENaC)
H+ via OTOP1 (sour) and Na+ via ENaC (salty)

questions.sub: Clinical Correlations
questions.q: A 74-year-old man who had a left occipital lobe stroke develops pure alexia (inability to read words), right homonymous hemianopsia, and right-sided hemiachromatopsia (loss of color perception in the right visual hemifield, seeing the right half of the world in shades of grey). Which ventral occipitotemporal area is damaged?
options: Left lingual and fusiform gyri (human color-processing area V4 in the ventral visual 'what' stream)
Right parietal lobe
Left precentral gyrus
Cerebellar vermis
questions.explain: Cerebral achromatopsia (cortical color blindness) localizes to area V4 in the ventral occipitotemporal cortex (lingual/fusiform gyri).

open.q: Name the ventral occipitotemporal visual area whose unilateral lesion produces contralateral hemiachromatopsia (cortical loss of color vision).
accept: Area V4 (lingual and fusiform gyri)
Visual area V4 (lingual/fusiform gyri)

questions.sub: Clinical Correlations
questions.q: A 63-year-old woman suffers bilateral strokes affecting the lateral parieto-occipital junction (area V5 / MT, middle temporal visual area). Her visual acuity, reading, and color vision are normal, yet she cannot perceive motion—moving cars appear as a series of frozen still photographs, and pouring tea looks like a frozen glacier ('akinetopsia'). Which visual stream is damaged?
options: Dorsal magnocellular ('where/how' motion-processing) stream terminating in area V5/MT
Ventral parvocellular ('what' form/color) stream
Retinohypothalamic circadian tract
Olfactory piriform cortex
questions.explain: Area V5/MT in the dorsal magnocellular pathway is specialized for visual motion perception; bilateral V5/MT damage causes motion blindness (akinetopsia).

open.q: Name the condition and cortical visual area damaged when a patient has intact form and color vision but perceives moving objects as frozen still frames.
accept: Akinetopsia (motion blindness); visual area V5 / MT (middle temporal area in the dorsal stream)
Akinetopsia; area V5/MT

questions.sub: Clinical Correlations
questions.q: A 25-year-old diver ascends too rapidly without equalizing ear pressure during descent, experiencing sudden severe ear pain followed by a 'pop,' relief of pain, and a small amount of blood from the external ear canal with mild conductive hearing loss. Otoscopy shows a clean perforation of the tympanic membrane. Why does a simple tympanic membrane perforation cause conductive hearing loss?
options: Loss of intact tympanic membrane surface area reduces the pressure amplification ratio onto the oval window, and sound waves strike both the oval and round windows nearly simultaneously (canceling the pressure gradient across the basilar membrane)
It destroys the cochlea and spiral ganglion permanently
It causes endolymph to drain out of the nose
It paralyzes the stapedius muscle
questions.explain: A tympanic membrane perforation reduces both the hydraulic area-ratio gain and the phase difference between the oval and round windows, producing a mild-to-moderate conductive hearing loss.

open.q: Explain the two acoustic reasons a tympanic membrane perforation produces conductive hearing loss.
accept: 1) Loss of effective vibrating tympanic membrane surface area reduces pressure amplification onto the stapes footplate, and 2) sound waves reach the round window directly without phase delay, canceling the pressure difference across the oval and round windows
Reduced tympanic surface area amplification and loss of phase difference between oval and round windows

questions.sub: Vision: Optics, Refraction, Accommodation, and Refractive Errors
questions.q: What is 'spherical aberration' versus 'chromatic aberration' in the human eye, and how does the iris reduce spherical aberration?
options: Spherical aberration occurs when peripheral light rays passing near the lens edge bend more strongly than central axial rays; pupillary constriction (miosis) blocks peripheral rays to sharpen focus; Chromatic aberration occurs because short-wavelength blue light refracts more strongly than long-wavelength red light
Red light bends twice as sharply as blue light in water
Pupillary dilation eliminates all spherical aberration completely
Chromatic aberration is caused by deafness in the left ear
questions.explain: Pupillary constriction during near vision (miosis in the near triad) blocks marginal peripheral rays, minimizing spherical aberration and increasing depth of field.

open.q: Explain how pupillary constriction (miosis) improves image sharpness during near vision.
accept: Blocking peripheral light rays passing through the edges of the cornea and lens reduces spherical aberration and increases depth of field
Blocks peripheral rays to reduce spherical aberration and increase depth of field

questions.sub: Vision: Retinal Layers, Rods vs Cones, and Phototransduction
questions.q: What is the 'Purkinje shift' observed as lighting transitions from bright daylight (photopic) to dim twilight (scotopic)?
options: Peak visual spectral sensitivity shifts from ~555 nm (yellow-green, dominated by M/L cones in daylight) toward ~500 nm (blue-green, dominated by rod rhodopsin in twilight), making blue flowers appear relatively brighter than red flowers at dusk
Peak visual sensitivity shifts into the far-infrared (>2,000 nm)
Rods take over reading fine newspaper print at noon
The iris changes color from brown to blue in bright sunlight
questions.explain: As cones drop out at dusk and rods (~500 nm rhodopsin peak) take over, shorter blue-green wavelengths appear subjectively brighter relative to long red wavelengths.

open.q: Define the Purkinje shift as illumination transitions from daylight to twilight.
accept: Shift in peak spectral sensitivity of the human eye from ~555 nm (yellow-green, cone-dominated) in bright light to ~500 nm (blue-green, rod-dominated) in dim light
Peak sensitivity shifts from ~555 nm (cones) in daylight to ~500 nm (rods) in twilight

questions.sub: Audition: Cochlear Mechanics, Organ of Corti, and Hair Cell Transduction
questions.q: What is 'masking' in auditory physiology, and why do low-frequency sounds mask high-frequency sounds much more effectively than high-frequency sounds mask low-frequency sounds ('upward spread of masking')?
options: Because a low-frequency traveling wave starts at the stiff basal turn and travels all the way to the apex (exciting basal high-frequency hair cells along its path), whereas a high-frequency wave peaks sharply at the base and dies out immediately without reaching the apex
High-frequency sounds vibrate the entire apex of the cochlea
Low-frequency sounds travel through the Eustachian tube into the throat
Masking occurs because the stapedius muscle contracts only to 15 kHz tones
questions.explain: Because every traveling wave enters at the basal oval window and sweeps apically until its resonant place, low-frequency basal tails overlap high-frequency basal regions ('upward spread of masking').

open.q: Explain why low-frequency sounds mask high-frequency sounds more strongly than vice versa along the basilar membrane.
accept: Low-frequency traveling waves pass through the basal (high-frequency) region of the basilar membrane on their way to the apex, whereas high-frequency waves peak and attenuate rapidly at the base without disturbing apical low-frequency regions
Low-frequency traveling waves sweep across the basal high-frequency region en route to the apex, while high-frequency waves die out at the base

questions.sub: Vestibular System: Semicircular Canals, Otolith Organs, and Nystagmus
questions.q: How do the 'vestibulospinal tracts' (lateral and medial) use otolith and semicircular canal inputs to prevent falling when you trip?
options: Lateral vestibulospinal: ipsilateral extensor tone; medial vestibulospinal: head/neck stabilisation
Vestibulospinal tracts inhibit all limb extensors so the person collapses immediately
Vestibulospinal tracts project exclusively to the primary visual cortex
Otolith organs inhibit the diaphragm during standing
questions.explain: Rapid otolith-vestibulospinal extensor reflexes extend the ipsilateral limb to catch your weight before conscious cortical awareness even registers a stumble. Key detail: When the head tilts suddenly, otolith and canal afferents excite the lateral vestibular nucleus (Deiters'), which drives the ipsilateral lateral vestibulospinal tract to strongly excite antigravity limb extensor motor neurons on the side of tilt while the medial vestibulospinal tract stabilizes head position via neck muscles.

open.q: State the functional roles of the lateral vestibulospinal tract and medial vestibulospinal tract in postural balance.
accept: Lateral vestibulospinal tract: excites ipsilateral antigravity limb extensor motor neurons to maintain upright posture; Medial vestibulospinal tract: coordinates cervical neck motor neurons to stabilize head position
Limb antigravity extensor tone (lateral vestibulospinal) and head/neck stabilization (medial vestibulospinal)

questions.sub: Gustation (Taste) and Olfaction (Smell) Transduction and Pathways
questions.q: What is 'sensory adaptation' across the special senses, and which special senses adapt rapidly versus very slowly?
options: Olfaction and cutaneous touch adapt rapidly (explaining why you stop noticing your own perfume or clothing within minutes), whereas nociceptors (pain) and vestibular/proprioceptive receptors adapt very slowly or not at all to maintain continuous protective and postural awareness
Pain receptors adapt completely within 2 seconds while olfaction never adapts
Photoreceptors never adapt to changes in room brightness
Taste buds permanently stop responding after tasting sugar once
questions.explain: Rapid olfactory adaptation (mediated by Ca2+-calmodulin desensitization of olfactory CNG channels and beta-arrestin receptor internalization) keeps the nose sensitive to new ambient odors.

open.q: Contrast the rate of sensory adaptation in olfaction versus nociception (pain) and explain the physiological advantage of each.
accept: Olfaction adapts rapidly (allowing detection of new environmental odors without background saturation), whereas nociception adapts slowly or not at all (providing continuous warning of ongoing tissue injury)
Rapid adaptation in olfaction (detects novel odors) vs minimal/slow adaptation in nociception (sustained tissue-damage warning)

questions.sub: Clinical Correlations
questions.q: A 36-year-old woman presents with a 3-month history of progressive hearing loss in her right ear. Weber test lateralizes to the right ear, and Rinne test shows Bone Conduction > Air Conduction on the right. Acoustic reflex testing shows absent stapedius reflex on the right. Which surgery restores ossicular sound transmission in otosclerosis?
options: Stapedectomy (or stapedotomy) with insertion of a prosthetic piston connecting the incus to the oval window
Enucleation of the right eye
Craniotomy for occipital lobectomy
Tonsillectomy
questions.explain: Replacing the immobilized stapes superstructure with a micro-prosthesis (stapedectomy/stapedotomy) restores mechanical vibration transfer from the incus to the oval window perilymph.

open.q: Name the microsurgical procedure used to restore conductive hearing in otosclerosis.
accept: Stapedectomy / stapedotomy (prosthetic replacement of the fixed stapes)
Stapedectomy

questions.sub: Clinical Correlations
questions.q: A 60-year-old man with hypertension and diabetes presents with sudden painless horizontal diplopia that worsens when looking to the LEFT. On exam, his left eye cannot abduct past the midline while all other eye movements and pupillary reflexes are normal. Which cranial nerve is affected and why is it especially vulnerable to intracranial hypertension?
options: Left Abducens nerve (CN VI) — its long intracranial subarachnoid course along the clivus and sharp bend over the petrous ridge (Dorello's canal) make CN VI vulnerable to stretching ('false localizing sign') when ICP rises, as well as diabetic microvascular ischemia
Right Oculomotor nerve (CN III)
Left Trochlear nerve (CN IV)
Right Optic nerve (CN II)
questions.explain: CN VI innervates the lateral rectus (abduction); its long tethered course along the clivus makes unilateral or bilateral CN VI palsy a classic 'false localizing sign' of elevated intracranial pressure.

open.q: Which cranial nerve is paralyzed when the left eye fails to abduct, and why is this nerve prone to 'false localizing' palsy during elevated intracranial pressure?
accept: Left abducens nerve (CN VI); its long subarachnoid path along the clivus and tethering in Dorello's canal cause downward brainstem displacement from high ICP to stretch the nerve
Left abducens nerve (CN VI); long tethered intracranial course along the clivus

questions.sub: Clinical Correlations
questions.q: A 51-year-old man who sustained a traumatic brain injury reports a distorted, foul, rotting smell ('cacosmia / parosmia') whenever he eats normal foods, and he has lost 8 kg due to food aversion. Which cranial nerve and cortical area process olfactory perception?
options: Olfactory nerve (CN I) projecting via the olfactory bulb and tract to the primary olfactory (piriform) cortex, amygdala, and orbitofrontal cortex
Glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) projecting to the occipital pole
Trigeminal nerve (CN V) projecting to Heschl's gyrus
Vestibulocochlear nerve (CN VIII) projecting to Broca's area
questions.explain: Aberrant regeneration of olfactory sensory axons after cribriform plate shearing trauma commonly produces distorted phantom/foul smells (parosmia/phantosmia).

open.q: Name the primary cortical area where olfactory tract fibers terminate to generate conscious smell perception.
accept: Primary olfactory cortex (piriform cortex, with projections to amygdala, entorhinal cortex, and orbitofrontal cortex)
Piriform (primary olfactory) cortex

questions.sub: Clinical Correlations
questions.q: A 7-year-old child with congenital bilateral profound sensorineural deafness due to non-functional cochlear hair cells is evaluated for a 'cochlear implant'. How does a cochlear implant restore auditory perception?
options: A cochlear electrode array stimulates spiral ganglion neurons, bypassing damaged hair cells
It amplifies airborne sound waves by 200 dB against the tympanic membrane
It replaces the cerebellar dentate nucleus
It stimulates the optic nerve to convert light into sound
questions.explain: Because a cochlear implant directly depolarizes spiral ganglion neurons along the tonotopic axis of the cochlea, it requires an intact auditory nerve (CN VIII) to succeed. Key detail: An external microphone and speech processor convert sound into frequency-filtered electrical pulses delivered directly via a tonotopically arranged electrode array inserted into the scala tympani to stimulate intact spiral ganglion (CN VIII) nerve fibers directly, bypassing damaged hair cells.

open.q: Explain how a cochlear implant bypasses damaged cochlear hair cells and which neural structure it stimulates directly.
accept: It converts sound into frequency-specific electrical impulses delivered via a tonotopic electrode array in the scala tympani to directly depolarize spiral ganglion (CN VIII) auditory nerve fibers
Tonotopic electrical stimulation of spiral ganglion (CN VIII) neurons in the scala tympani, bypassing damaged hair cells

questions.sub: Clinical Correlations
questions.q: A 32-year-old woman with systemic lupus erythematosus treated with high-dose hydroxychloroquine for 9 years develops progressive bilateral paracentral visual field loss ('bull's-eye maculopathy') with impaired color discrimination. Which retinal cells are damaged by hydroxychloroquine retinal toxicity?
options: Retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) and parafoveal cone/rod photoreceptors
Corneal endothelial cells only
Lacrimal gland acinar cells
Lateral rectus skeletal muscle fibers
questions.explain: Hydroxychloroquine binds melanin in the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), causing progressive RPE and photoreceptor degeneration in a classic ring ('bull's-eye') around the fovea.

open.q: Which retinal structures are damaged in hydroxychloroquine-induced 'bull's-eye maculopathy'?
accept: Retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) and parafoveal photoreceptors
Retinal pigment epithelium and photoreceptors

questions.sub: Optics of the eye
questions.q: Which structure provides most of the refractive power of the eye?
options: Cornea
Lens
Vitreous humour
Aqueous humour
questions.explain: The air-cornea interface gives about 43 of the eye's 59 dioptres. The lens adds the smaller, adjustable part, so students often wrongly pick it.

open.q: Which structure provides most of the refractive power of the eye?
accept: Anterior surface of the eye
Transparent front of the eyeball
Corneal surface

questions.sub: Optics of the eye
questions.q: Which muscle contracts to make the lens rounder for near vision?
options: Sphincter pupillae
Ciliary muscle
Medial rectus
Dilator pupillae
questions.explain: Contraction of the ciliary muscle slackens the zonular fibres, so the elastic lens becomes more convex. The medial rectus contributes convergence, not lens shape.

open.q: Which muscle of the eye contracts to increase the curvature of the lens during accommodation?
accept: Ciliaris
Ciliary body muscle
Muscle of the ciliary body

questions.sub: Retina and phototransduction
questions.q: Red-green colour blindness is inherited in which pattern?
options: Autosomal dominant
Autosomal recessive
Mitochondrial
X-linked recessive
questions.explain: The genes for the red and green cone opsins lie on the X chromosome. About 8% of males are affected, but few females.

open.q: What is the inheritance pattern of red-green colour blindness?
accept: Sex-linked recessive
Carried on the X chromosome
Affects mostly males through carrier mothers

questions.sub: Optics of the eye
questions.q: Which type of lens is used to correct myopia?
options: Convex lens
Cylindrical lens
Concave lens
Prism lens
questions.explain: In myopia the image falls in front of the retina. A diverging concave lens moves the focus back onto the retina.

open.q: Which type of lens is used to correct myopia?
accept: Diverging lens
Minus lens
Negative lens

questions.sub: Optics of the eye
questions.q: In an uncorrected hypermetropic eye with accommodation relaxed, where is the image of a distant object focused?
options: In front of the retina
Behind the retina
At two focal lines
On the macula
questions.explain: The eyeball is too short or the refractive power too weak, so rays focus behind the retina. Convex lenses correct it, and a young person can compensate by accommodating.
