open.q: In an uncorrected hypermetropic eye with accommodation relaxed, where is the image of a distant object focused?
accept: Posterior to the retina
Beyond the retina
Behind the macula

questions.sub: Optics of the eye
questions.q: What is the main cause of presbyopia?
options: Increased corneal curvature
Raised intraocular pressure
Loss of lens elasticity
Shortened eyeball length
questions.explain: With age the lens stiffens and cannot become rounder, so the near point recedes. It usually becomes noticeable after about 40 years.

open.q: What is the main cause of presbyopia?
accept: Lens hardening with age
Reduced lens elasticity
Age-related stiffening of the lens

questions.sub: Retina and phototransduction
questions.q: Which photoreceptors are responsible for vision in dim light?
options: Rods
Cones
Ganglion cells
Amacrine cells
questions.explain: Rods contain rhodopsin and are very sensitive to light, but they give no colour vision. Cones work in bright light.

open.q: Which photoreceptors are responsible for vision in dim light?
accept: Rod cells
Scotopic photoreceptors
Night vision receptors

questions.sub: Retina and phototransduction
questions.q: Which part of the retina provides the highest visual acuity?
options: Optic disc
Ora serrata
Peripheral retina
Fovea centralis
questions.explain: The fovea has densely packed cones with almost one-to-one connections to ganglion cells, and the overlying layers are displaced to the side. The optic disc is the blind spot.

open.q: Which part of the retina provides the highest visual acuity?
accept: Macula lutea
Central pit of the retina
Foveola

questions.sub: Retina and phototransduction
questions.q: How does light change the membrane potential of a rod photoreceptor?
options: Action potential firing
Depolarisation
Hyperpolarisation
No change in potential
questions.explain: In darkness cGMP keeps sodium channels open and the rod is partly depolarised. Light lowers cGMP, the channels close and the rod hyperpolarises, releasing less glutamate.

open.q: How does light change the membrane potential of a rod photoreceptor?
accept: Becomes more negative
Graded response with less glutamate release
Closure of cGMP-gated channels

questions.sub: Retina and phototransduction
questions.q: Which molecule changes from the 11-cis to the all-trans form when rhodopsin absorbs a photon?
options: Opsin
Transducin
cGMP
Retinal
questions.explain: Isomerisation of retinal activates opsin, which activates transducin and starts the cascade that lowers cGMP.

open.q: Which molecule changes from the 11-cis to the all-trans form when rhodopsin absorbs a photon?
accept: Retinaldehyde
Vitamin A aldehyde
Chromophore of rhodopsin

questions.sub: Retina and phototransduction
questions.q: Deficiency of which vitamin causes night blindness?
options: Vitamin A
Vitamin B12
Vitamin C
Vitamin E
questions.explain: Vitamin A is needed to form retinal. Without it rhodopsin cannot be regenerated, so vision in dim light is impaired.

open.q: Deficiency of which vitamin causes night blindness?
accept: Retinol
Retinol deficiency
Fat-soluble vitamin that forms retinal

questions.sub: Retina and phototransduction
questions.q: Which retinal neurons are the only output cells of the retina?
options: Bipolar cells
Amacrine cells
Ganglion cells
Horizontal cells
questions.explain: Axons of the ganglion cells form the optic nerve. The other retinal neurons only modify the signal within the retina.

open.q: Which retinal neurons are the only output cells of the retina?
accept: Retinal ganglion cells
Cells forming the optic nerve
Neurons that fire action potentials in the retina

questions.sub: Visual pathway
questions.q: Fibres from which part of each retina cross at the optic chiasm?
options: Nasal half
Temporal half
Upper half
Macular region only
questions.explain: Nasal fibres carry the temporal visual field and cross to the opposite optic tract. Temporal fibres stay on the same side.

open.q: Fibres from which half of each retina cross at the optic chiasm?
accept: Medial half of the retina
Fibres carrying the temporal visual field
Half nearer the nose

questions.sub: Visual pathway
questions.q: A man with a pituitary adenoma bumps into objects on both sides. Which visual field defect is present?
options: Binasal hemianopia
Homonymous hemianopia
Bitemporal hemianopia
Central scotoma
questions.explain: The tumour compresses the optic chiasm and damages the crossing nasal fibres, so both temporal fields are lost. Homonymous defects arise from lesions behind the chiasm.

open.q: A man with a pituitary adenoma bumps into objects on both sides. Which visual field defect is present?
accept: Loss of both temporal visual fields
Chiasmal syndrome field defect
Heteronymous temporal hemianopia

questions.sub: Visual pathway
questions.q: A stroke damages the right optic tract. Which visual field defect results?
options: Right monocular blindness
Bitemporal hemianopia
Right homonymous hemianopia
Left homonymous hemianopia
questions.explain: The right tract carries fibres from the right temporal retina and the left nasal retina. Together they represent the left visual field, so that field is lost in both eyes.

open.q: A stroke damages the right optic tract. Which visual field defect results?
accept: Loss of the left visual field in both eyes
Contralateral homonymous hemianopia
Left-sided field loss in both eyes

questions.sub: Visual pathway
questions.q: Light shone into one eye also constricts the pupil of the other eye. Which midbrain structures send bilateral projections to the Edinger-Westphal nuclei to produce this?
options: Lateral geniculate nuclei
Pretectal nuclei
Superior colliculi
Occipital cortex
questions.explain: Optic tract fibres synapse in the pretectal nuclei, which project to both Edinger-Westphal nuclei. This explains the consensual light reflex, which does not use the visual cortex.

open.q: Light shone into one eye also constricts the pupil of the other eye. Which midbrain structures send bilateral projections to the Edinger-Westphal nuclei to produce this?
accept: Pretectal area
Midbrain pretectum
Olivary pretectal nucleus

questions.sub: Visual pathway
questions.q: A patient has ptosis, a dilated pupil that does not react to light and an eye turned down and out. Which cranial nerve is damaged?
options: Abducens nerve
Trochlear nerve
Oculomotor nerve
Trigeminal nerve
questions.explain: The oculomotor nerve supplies levator palpebrae, most extraocular muscles and the parasympathetic fibres to the pupil. The unopposed lateral rectus and superior oblique pull the eye down and out.

open.q: A patient has ptosis, a dilated pupil that does not react to light and an eye turned down and out. Which cranial nerve is damaged?
accept: Cranial nerve III
Third cranial nerve
CN III

questions.sub: Hearing
questions.q: What is the main function of the tympanic membrane and ossicular chain?
options: Filtering out high-frequency background noise
Matching the impedance of air to cochlear fluid
Equalising air pressure on both sides of the drum
Determining the direction of the sound source
questions.explain: The large drum area and the lever action of the ossicles concentrate pressure on the small oval window, overcoming the loss of energy at the air-to-fluid boundary. The eustachian tube equalises pressure.

open.q: What is the main function of the tympanic membrane and ossicular chain?
accept: Amplifying sound pressure for the oval window
Pressure transformation between air and fluid
Overcoming the air-to-fluid loss of sound energy

questions.sub: Hearing
questions.q: Paralysis of which nerve causes hyperacusis because the stapedius reflex is lost?
options: Trigeminal nerve
Vagus nerve
